Exercises

Exercise 12.1 — The ratio, by hand

Using zlens=0.3266z_{\mathrm{lens}} = 0.3266 and zsrc=0.7497z_{\mathrm{src}} = 0.7497, compute zsrc/zlensz_{\mathrm{src}}/z_{\mathrm{lens}} and state whether this DESI pair would survive Hsu et al. (2025)’s friends-of-friends discovery cut.

Solution

0.7497/0.3266=2.29540.7497 / 0.3266 = 2.2954, comfortably above the threshold of 1.31.3. The pair survives — it is, in fact, one of the 13,530 groups the cut keeps at full DR1 scale.

Exercise 12.2 — Why Balmer-alpha doesn’t work here

Compute where Balmer-alpha (rest wavelength 6564.61 Å) would land if you searched for it in the source spectrum at zsrc=0.7497z_{\mathrm{src}} = 0.7497. Then explain why a redshift pipeline does not simply fail when one expected line falls outside the observable band.

Solution

6564.61×1.7497=11486.156564.61 \times 1.7497 = 11486.15 Å , deep in the near-infrared — well outside where a ground-based optical spectrograph is sensitive, compared to the 5218–6522 Å range where the Ca II K and [OII] lines in this chapter’s worked example actually landed. The pipeline does not fail, because it never depended on any one line: it cross-correlates a whole template (Ch. 7’s operation) against the data, and at any given zz some other line in the template — with a different rest wavelength — falls inside the band instead.

Exercise 12.3 — Shift vs. width, by the numbers

Using σv=217.09\sigma_v = 217.09 km/s on the Ca II K line, verify Δλwidth≈2.85\Delta\lambda_{\text{width}} \approx 2.85 Å. Compare it to the shift computed for the same line, 5218.47−3933.665218.47 - 3933.66 Å. What is the ratio, and what does it tell you about why a redshift is visible by eye but a velocity dispersion is not?

Solution

Δλwidth=3933.66×(217.09/299792.458)=2.848\Delta\lambda_{\text{width}} = 3933.66 \times (217.09/299792.458) = 2.848 Å . The shift is 5218.47−3933.66=1284.815218.47 - 3933.66 = 1284.81 Å. The ratio is about 450: the shift displaces a line across more than a thousand Ångstroms, while the width perturbs it by less than three — a scale comparable to the spectrograph’s own resolution element. That is why zz is legible on a plotted spectrum and σv\sigma_v requires fitting the line profile against an instrumental-resolution model.

Exercise 12.4 — The fitter’s cap

9,292 of Hsu et al.’s 13,530 candidate pairs lack a trustworthy σv\sigma_v. What fraction of the whole sample is that? If an analysis used FastSpecFit’s VDISP column without checking VDISP_IVAR > 0, why can’t you simply look at the number 250.0 km/s and know it’s a placeholder rather than a real measurement?

Solution

9292/13530=0.6879292 / 13530 = 0.687, about 68.7% of the sample. You can’t tell a real 250 km/s from the fitter’s failure cap by inspecting the value alone — 250 km/s is a perfectly ordinary velocity dispersion for a massive elliptical (reproductions/hsu-2025/07_classify_einstein_dimple.py:145-153). The only way to distinguish them is the diagnostic that ships alongside the number, VDISP_IVAR: zero means the fit gave up and returned its template floor, not a measurement.

13. The expanding universe and redshift

This chapter answers a question every redshift number in this repository quietly assumes you can already read: what does zz mean? Cikota’s Einstein cross, the Carousel cluster’s background sheet, Ch. 12’s DESI fiber-pair search — every one of them reports zz as if its meaning were obvious. By the end of this chapter you can say exactly what it asserts about the universe itself, derive Hubble’s law from a single Taylor expansion — the same move Ch. 02 promised would recur through the whole book — and explain precisely why H0=70H_0 = 70 is not, on its own, an age or a speed limit.

What you can skip

Of the whole book, this chapter and the two after it (Ch. 14, Ch. 15) are the most detachable. The lens-modelling likelihood this repository actually optimises — the one Ch. 22 through Ch. 26 build up in full — is entirely angular: arcseconds in, arcseconds out, with no cosmological quantity anywhere in its gradient (site/guide_src/cosmo.py:4). Cosmology enters this repository’s campaigns only where a physical, non-angular scale is required, and the money-number pipeline is not one of those places — see “Connect to the repo” below for the full, short list. If your only goal is γ=1.103\gamma = 1.103 , skip straight to Ch. 16. Read this chapter instead before your first meeting with an astronomer: “the universe is expanding” is the one sentence every one of them assumes you already hold for the right reasons, and after this chapter, you will.

The scale factor

Cosmologists describe the universe’s size with a single dimensionless function of time, the scale factor a(t)a(t), normalized so that a(t0)≡1a(t_0) \equiv 1 today, at t0t_0. It carries no units and no meaning in isolation — only the ratio of aa at two different times means anything, and that ratio is exactly what a measured redshift hands you, in the next section.

The picture underneath a(t)a(t): lay a fixed grid over the universe, with galaxies (on average, ignoring their small individual peculiar motions) sitting at fixed grid coordinates for all time — their comoving positions, 𝐱c\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{c}}. Nothing on this grid moves. What changes is the ruler: the physical (proper) distance between two grid points at time tt is

dphys(t)=a(t)dc, d_{\mathrm{phys}}(t) \;=\; a(t)\, d_{\mathrm{c}},

where dcd_{\mathrm{c}} is the fixed comoving separation between them. At t=t0t = t_0, a=1a = 1 and physical distance equals comoving distance — exactly why the normalization was chosen that way.

You already know this

A comoving coordinate is a fixed label — like a vertex stored in normalized device coordinates, unchanged by anything downstream. The scale factor a(t)a(t) is the single global multiplier that turns those fixed labels into physical distances at time tt, the same way a viewport transform turns NDC into pixels. The mesh — every galaxy’s comoving position — never moves. Only the multiplier changes, uniformly, everywhere, at once.

a(t)a(t)’s actual functional form — whether it grows like t2/3t^{2/3}, accelerates, or does something else entirely — is set by how much matter and dark energy the universe holds, and deriving it is Ch. 14’s job. This chapter needs only a(t)a(t)’s value today and its instantaneous rate of change right now — and that rate of change is exactly what “H0=70H_0 = 70” reports.

Hubble’s law

Define the Hubble parameter as the log-derivative of the scale factor,

H(t)≡ȧ(t)a(t)=ddtln⁡a(t). H(t) \;\equiv\; \frac{\dot a(t)}{a(t)} \;=\; \frac{d}{dt}\ln a(t).

This is exactly the quantity you would call a continuously-compounded growth rate in any other setting: the fractional change in size per unit time, evaluated instantaneously. a(t)a(t) need not actually grow exponentially — H(t)H(t) is a snapshot of its rate at tt, not a claim about its long-run shape.

Taylor-expand a(t)a(t) to first order around today, t0t_0, exactly as Ch. 02 does for every other hard object in this book:

a(t)≈1+H0(t−t0),H0≡H(t0), a(t) \;\approx\; 1 \;+\; H_0\,(t - t_0), \qquad H_0 \equiv H(t_0), \label{eq:a-taylor}

using a(t0)=1a(t_0) = 1. This is nothing but a derivative given a name: the slope of the line tangent to a(t)a(t) at t0t_0.

Now put a comoving galaxy at fixed comoving distance dcd_{\mathrm{c}}. Its proper distance at any nearby time is d(t)=a(t)dcd(t) = a(t)\, d_{\mathrm{c}}, so its recession velocity is

v(t)=ddt[a(t)dc]=ȧ(t)dc=ȧ(t)a(t)[a(t)dc]=H(t)d(t). v(t) \;=\; \frac{d}{dt}\big[a(t)\, d_{\mathrm{c}}\big] \;=\; \dot a(t)\, d_{\mathrm{c}} \;=\; \frac{\dot a(t)}{a(t)}\,\big[a(t)\, d_{\mathrm{c}}\big] \;=\; H(t)\, d(t).

Evaluated today, this is Hubble’s law, v=H0dv = H_0\, d. It is not an empirical fit stapled onto the expansion after the fact; it is $\eqref{eq:a-taylor}$’s linear term, restated as a velocity instead of a scale factor.

Everywhere this repository touches cosmology, it fixes H0=70H_0 = 70 km/s/Mpc (site/guide_src/cosmo.py:29). What else the model carries — Ωm\Omega_m, dark energy — is Ch. 14’s subject; only H0H_0 matters here. The units are the tell: velocity over distance is 1/time1/\text{time}, a rate, not a speed and not a length. Two readings of that rate:

  • Hubble time, 1/H0=13.971/H_0 = 13.97 Gyr — roughly the age of the universe, though not exactly; Ch. 14 derives why the two differ once matter and dark energy get a vote in a(t)a(t)’s history.
  • Hubble distance, c/H0=4283c/H_0 = 4283 Mpc — the characteristic length scale of the observable universe.

Equivalently, H0H_0 itself is 0.07160.0716 per Gyr: at today’s rate, every comoving distance grows about seven percent larger per billion years — the same dln⁡a/dtd\ln a/dt from above, in units a human timescale can hold.

Redshift as expansion

A photon is a wave, and as it crosses expanding space its wavelength is carried along by the same scale factor that carries a comoving distance:

λobsλemit=a(tobs)a(temit)=1a(temit), \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{emit}}} \;=\; \frac{a(t_{\mathrm{obs}})}{a(t_{\mathrm{emit}})} \;=\; \frac{1}{a(t_{\mathrm{emit}})},

using a(tobs)=a(t0)≡1a(t_{\mathrm{obs}}) = a(t_0) \equiv 1, since “observed” means “now.” Ch. 12 already showed you how zz gets measured — as exactly this wavelength ratio, off a spectral line whose rest wavelength is known from the lab. Define it the same way here:

1+z≡λobsλemit=1a(temit),a(temit)=11+z. 1 + z \;\equiv\; \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{emit}}} \;=\; \frac{1}{a(t_{\mathrm{emit}})}, \qquad a(t_{\mathrm{emit}}) = \frac{1}{1+z}.

That is the whole content of “redshift is expansion”: a measured zz is a direct readout of how large the universe was when the light in front of you left its source, relative to how large it is now. Not a velocity through space — a size, then, compared against a size, now.

Four redshifts already sitting in this repository’s worked examples translate directly:

system zz a(temit)=1/(1+z)a(t_{\mathrm{emit}}) = 1/(1+z)
Cikota+2023 Einstein-cross lens 0.271 0.787
Cikota+2023 Einstein-cross source 0.897 0.527
Carousel cluster lens (Ch. 15) 0.49 0.671
Carousel reference plane 1.432 0.411

The last row is the sharpest teaching example. It is tempting to read zz as a velocity via v≈czv \approx cz — and at low zz that is a good approximation, since it is exactly $\eqref{eq:a-taylor}$’s linear term again, this time along the photon’s path instead of a nearby galaxy’s worldline. Push it past where the linear approximation holds and it breaks outright: read the Carousel’s own zref=1.432z_{\mathrm{ref}} = 1.432 as “czcz” and you get 429,303 km/s, i.e. 1.432c1.432\,c — faster than light. Nothing travels that fast, and nothing has to: no object is moving through space at all, space itself is stretching, and there is no speed limit on how fast a purely geometric distance can grow — the same way there is no upper bound on how fast a resized window can grow even though nothing drawn inside it is “moving.” The correct statement was never a velocity. It is a(temit)=0.411a(t_{\mathrm{emit}}) = 0.411: the universe was 41 percent its current size when that light left.

  • site/guide_src/cosmo.py:4 states the audit this chapter’s skip-box leans on: the lens-modelling likelihood is entirely angular, and cosmology enters campaigns in this repository only at a short, enumerated list of places:

    • reproductions/sheu-2024b/04_setup_multiplane.py:35 — Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} and M(<θE)M(<\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) for the Carousel cluster, worked in full in Ch. 15.

Exercises

Exercise 13.1 — Hubble’s law, both directions

Starting from $\eqref{eq:a-taylor}$, derive v=H0dv = H_0 d for a nearby comoving galaxy (two lines of algebra suffice). Then use it to predict the recession velocity of a galaxy at d=100d = 100 Mpc, and invert v≈czv \approx cz to get the redshift that recession velocity implies.

Solution

Differentiate d(t)=a(t)dcd(t) = a(t)\, d_{\mathrm{c}}: ḋ=ȧdc=(ȧ/a)(adc)=H(t)d(t)\dot d = \dot a\, d_{\mathrm{c}} = (\dot a/a)\,(a\, d_{\mathrm{c}}) = H(t)\, d(t). At t=t0t = t_0, H(t0)=H0H(t_0) = H_0 and d(t0)=dd(t_0) = d, so v=H0dv = H_0 d.

At d=100d = 100 Mpc: v=70×100=7000v = 70 \times 100 = 7000 km/s. Inverting v≈czv \approx cz: z≈v/c≈0.0233z \approx v/c \approx 0.0233. This is the same linear regime the naive-czcz trap in “Redshift as expansion” breaks out of once zz stops being small.

Exercise 13.2 — Two scale factors you will need again

Compute a(temit)=1/(1+z)a(t_{\mathrm{emit}}) = 1/(1+z) for z=0.5z = 0.5 and z=2.0z = 2.0. Ch. 15 uses exactly this pair to show that angular-diameter distances do not subtract. State in one sentence what each scale factor means physically.

Solution

a(0.5)=1/1.5=0.667a(0.5) = 1/1.5 = 0.667. a(2.0)=1/3=0.333a(2.0) = 1/3 = 0.333. The z=0.5z=0.5 light left when the universe was two-thirds its current size; the z=2.0z=2.0 light left when it was one-third — a factor of two in redshift is not a factor of two in “how far back,” because aa and zz are related by 1/(1+z)1/(1+z), not linearly.

Exercise 13.3 — Why c/H0c/H_0 has units of length

H0H_0 is quoted in km/s/Mpc. Show, by unit algebra alone, that c/H0c/H_0 has units of length, then compute it and compare it to the Hubble distance quoted above.

Solution

[c]/[H0]=(km/s)/(km s−1Mpc−1)=Mpc[c]/[H_0] = (\text{km/s}) / (\text{km s}^{-1}\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}) = \text{Mpc} — the km/s cancels completely, leaving a pure length. Numerically, c/H0=4283c/H_0 = 4283 Mpc, matching the Hubble distance quoted in “Hubble’s law” above. Run the same cancellation on 1/H01/H_0 instead and what is left is a pure time — the Hubble time.

Exercise 13.4 — The naive-czcz trap, generalised

The Carousel’s reference redshift, read as czcz, gave 1.432c1.432\,c — faster than light. At roughly what redshift does the naive Newtonian reading v=czv = cz first predict a superluminal recession, and why does crossing that threshold not violate special relativity?

Solution

v=czv = cz exceeds cc as soon as z>1z > 1 — no computation needed beyond noticing cz>c⇔z>1cz > c \iff z > 1. Both the Carousel’s reference plane (zref=1.432z_{\mathrm{ref}} = 1.432) and the naive-czcz speed derived from it (429,303 km/s) sit past that threshold. Special relativity bounds the speed of anything moving through space; it says nothing about how fast a purely geometric distance between two points can grow while nothing moves through the space in between. v=czv = cz is only ever the low-zz approximation to a(temit)=1/(1+z)a(t_{\mathrm{emit}}) = 1/(1+z) — the actual, always-valid statement — so its failure at high zz is the approximation’s fault, not relativity’s.

14. FRW and the Friedmann equations

Chapter 13 gave you the scale factor a(t)a(t) and showed that redshift is a record of how much aa has grown since a photon left its source. This chapter gives you the equation that decides how a(t)a(t) actually evolves — the Friedmann equation — and the handful of numbers, Ωm\Omega_m and ΩΛ\Omega_\Lambda, that fix its trajectory. By the end you can write down FlatLambdaCDM(H0=70, Om0=0.3), the one line this repository’s cosmology begins and ends with, and say exactly what each of its two arguments asserts, including the third number it fixes that you never typed.

What you can skip

If you already have a GR or cosmology course behind you: skip the Newtonian derivation of the Friedmann equation below (you already have the real one from Einstein’s field equations) and the review of F=GMm/r2F = GMm/r^2. Go straight to The density parameters, where the only repo-specific content lives — what FlatLambdaCDM(70, 0.3) fixes, and the fact that Ωm+ΩΛ=1\Omega_m + \Omega_\Lambda = 1 is a definition, not a measurement (the measurement is that Ωk=0\Omega_k = 0). If you’re willing to take the Friedmann equation on faith entirely, skip to Connect to the repo: none of this chapter touches γ\gamma, and that fact is worth knowing on its own.

The FRW metric

A metric is a distance formula: a rule for turning a small coordinate separation into a physical (proper) length. In flat 2-D Euclidean space you already know it as ds2=dx2+dy2ds^2 = dx^2 + dy^2 — Pythagoras, applied to infinitesimally close points. General relativity’s only real complication is that the coefficients in that formula are allowed to depend on where, and when, you are.

You already know this

A metric is a (possibly position- or time-dependent) quadratic form that turns coordinate differences into a distance. That is exactly the job a covariance-weighted norm does when you whiten a feature vector, and it is exactly the job the mass matrix does in Ch. 23’s HMC sampler, which turns a gradient into a step in parameter space. The FRW metric below is the same kind of object, applied to spacetime.

The cosmological principle — on large scales the universe looks the same at every point (homogeneous) and the same in every direction from that point (isotropic) — is an assumption, well tested but unprovable in general. It is also an enormous constraint: it says the distance formula for the whole universe can depend on time through only one function and on space through only one constant. That function is a(t)a(t). The constant is a curvature index kk. The result is the Friedmann–Robertson–Walker (FRW) metric:

ds2=−c2dt2+a(t)2[dr21−kr2+r2dΩ2] ds^2 = -c^2\,dt^2 + a(t)^2\left[\frac{dr^2}{1-kr^2} + r^2\,d\Omega^2\right]

Here tt is cosmic time — the clock every observer at rest relative to the overall expansion agrees on — and rr is a comoving radial coordinate: fixed for an object that moves only with the Hubble flow, exactly the coordinate whose separation a(t)a(t) stretches into a physical one in Ch. 13. The term dΩ2d\Omega^2 is the ordinary solid-angle piece from spherical coordinates — the same combination you’d get unrolling latitude and longitude on a globe. This guide does not write out its two angles individually: those two symbols are reserved elsewhere for the lens-plane position (Ch. 17), and this repo’s overloading habit is exactly what this notation is trying to avoid repeating.

kk takes one of three values (after an overall rescaling of rr): k=−1k=-1 (open, hyperbolic, infinite volume), k=0k=0 (flat, ordinary Euclidean geometry), or k=+1k=+1 (closed, a 3-sphere, finite volume). This repository never considers the first or the third: every cosmology object it builds is FlatLambdaCDM, which hard-codes k=0k=0 and does not expose a curvature argument at all. Comoving coordinates are the ones a galaxy catalog is built in; the proper separation between two comoving points at a fixed time is a(t)a(t) times their (constant) comoving separation — the same idea Ch. 13 introduced for a single photon’s wavelength, now embedded in an actual distance formula. Ch. 15 turns this into the angular-diameter distance the lensing code calls directly.

Deriving this metric from Einstein’s field equations requires the tensor calculus this guide deliberately skips. You do not need that derivation to use the metric — you need it to know what makes a(t)a(t) move, which is the subject of the next section.

The Friedmann equation, derived as energy conservation

You can get the right equation for ȧ\dot a without any tensor calculus, using nothing but Newtonian energy conservation — a genuine, standard trick, not a hand-wave, though it comes with a caveat stated at the end of this section.

Pick any comoving observer as an origin and consider a sphere around them of fixed comoving radius rcr_c, small enough that space inside it looks uniform. Its physical radius is R(t)=a(t)rcR(t) = a(t)\,r_c, and by homogeneity it encloses a uniform matter density ρ(t)\rho(t), hence a mass M(R)=43πR3ρM(R) = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \rho. Put a test particle of mass mm on its surface. By Newton’s shell theorem the sphere pulls on that particle exactly as if all its mass sat at the center, so ordinary energy conservation gives

12mṘ2−GM(R)mR=E\frac{1}{2}m\dot R^2 - \frac{GM(R)m}{R} = E

with EE constant — nothing is adding or removing energy from the particle. Substituting M(R)M(R) and writing the (still-constant) EE in the suggestive form E≡−12mkc2rc2E \equiv -\frac{1}{2}mkc^2 r_c^2:

12Ṙ2−43πGρR2=−12kc2rc2\frac{1}{2}\dot R^2 - \frac{4}{3}\pi G\rho R^2 = -\frac{1}{2}kc^2 r_c^2

Divide through by 12R2=12a2rc2\frac{1}{2}R^2 = \frac{1}{2}a^2 r_c^2. The comoving radius rcr_c — which was arbitrary, the radius of a sphere you drew, not a physical scale — cancels completely, because Ṙ/R=ȧ/a\dot R/R = \dot a/a for any rcr_c. That cancellation is not a bookkeeping convenience; it is required, because the resulting law has to hold for every comoving observer, not just the one who happens to sit at the center of your particular sphere. What survives is the first Friedmann equation:

H2≡(ȧa)2=8πG3ρ−kc2a2 \begin{equation}\label{eq:friedmann} H^2 \equiv \left(\frac{\dot a}{a}\right)^2 = \frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho - \frac{kc^2}{a^2} \end{equation}

with the same curvature index kk that appears in the metric. A denser universe (ρ\rho larger) expands faster; positive curvature (k=+1k=+1) is a literal drag term that can eventually halt and reverse the expansion, exactly as positive total energy versus a negative one decides whether a thrown ball escapes to infinity or falls back.

The honest caveat. This derivation is Newtonian, and Newtonian gravity has no curvature and no dynamical role for pressure. That $\eqref{eq:friedmann}$ comes out exactly right is a genuine feature of general relativity applied to a homogeneous, isotropic spacetime (a cousin of Birkhoff’s theorem), not a coincidence you should distrust — but it is also not a proof, and it does not extend to the second Friedmann equation, the one governing ä\ddot a, which needs pressure to source gravity. Pressure gravitating at all has no Newtonian analogue; it is a genuinely relativistic effect, in the same family as the factor of two you’ll meet in Ch. 16 when light bends twice as far as Newton predicts. This repo never needs the second equation: it treats dark energy as a fixed extra density, not as the solution of a dynamical equation, which is exactly the next paragraph.

Adding dark energy and matter dilution. Treat the cosmological constant Λ\Lambda as an extra density component that never dilutes, ρΛ≡Λc2/(8πG)=const\rho_\Lambda \equiv \Lambda c^2/(8\pi G) = \text{const} — this capital Λ\Lambda is unrelated to the lowercase tempering parameter λ\lambda you’ll meet in Ch. 23; case is the only thing distinguishing them, so read carefully. Ordinary matter, by contrast, does dilute: mass conservation in a fixed comoving sphere, M=ρm(t)⋅43πR(t)3=constM = \rho_m(t)\cdot\frac{4}{3}\pi R(t)^3 = \text{const} (nothing creates or destroys matter, only accumulation the way Ch. 3 already had you doing over a volume), together with R∝aR \propto a, forces ρm(t)∝a(t)−3\rho_m(t) \propto a(t)^{-3}. Put both pieces into $\eqref{eq:friedmann}$ with ρ=ρm+ρΛ\rho = \rho_m + \rho_\Lambda.

A reference density. At any moment, relabel the right-hand side’s overall scale as a density: ρcrit(t)≡3H(t)28πG\rho_{\mathrm{crit}}(t) \equiv \dfrac{3H(t)^2}{8\pi G}. This is not a special density in the physics — it is what ρ\rho would have to equal for k=0k=0 to hold exactly at that instant, given the HH that instant actually has. It is the natural yardstick for the next section, and it is already enough to compute two numbers with only H0H_0 in hand. This repository fixes H0=70H_0 = 70 km/s/Mpc in every one of the three places cosmology appears (the next section names them), giving

ρcrit,0=3H028πG≈1.360×1011M⊙/Mpc3\rho_{\mathrm{crit,0}} = \frac{3H_0^2}{8\pi G} \approx 1.360\times10^{11}\ M_\odot / \text{Mpc}^3

— roughly one solar mass smeared over a cube 634 light-years on a side, which is the density the entire observable universe would need, on average, to be spatially flat. Ch. 13 already showed you the companion length and time scales that come from H0H_0 alone, the Hubble distance and Hubble time; ρcrit,0\rho_{\mathrm{crit,0}} is the third such scale, and it is the one that needs a density, not just a rate, to define.

Omega_m, Omega_Lambda, and what flat means

Normalize any density by ρcrit\rho_{\mathrm{crit}} and you get a dimensionless density parameter: Ωm≡ρm,0/ρcrit,0\Omega_m \equiv \rho_{m,0}/\rho_{\mathrm{crit,0}}, ΩΛ≡ρΛ/ρcrit,0\Omega_\Lambda \equiv \rho_{\Lambda}/\rho_{\mathrm{crit,0}}, and, folding the curvature term into the same units, Ωk≡−kc2/(H02a02)\Omega_k \equiv -kc^2/(H_0^2 a_0^2) (with the convention a0≡a(t0)=1a_0 \equiv a(t_0) = 1 today). Evaluate $\eqref{eq:friedmann}$ at t=t0t=t_0 and divide every term by H02H_0^2:

Ωm+ΩΛ+Ωk=1\Omega_m + \Omega_\Lambda + \Omega_k = 1

This identity costs you nothing: it is what dividing the Friedmann equation by H02H_0^2 always produces, for any universe, whatever its actual curvature. It is not evidence that the universe is flat. Flatness is the separate, empirical claim that Ωk=0\Omega_k = 0 — that curvature’s contribution happens to vanish. Once you assert that, the identity above collapses to Ωm+ΩΛ=1\Omega_m + \Omega_\Lambda = 1, and specifying Ωm\Omega_m alone fixes ΩΛ\Omega_\Lambda for free.

What FlatLambdaCDM(70, 0.3) actually asserts. Three independent places in this repository build the identical cosmology object: FlatLambdaCDM(H0=70, Om0=0.3), at reproductions/hsu-2025/07_classify_einstein_dimple.py:50 (source), reproductions/sheu-2024b/04_setup_multiplane.py:35 (source), and reproductions/sheu-2023/05_lightcurve_salt3.py:57 (source). That one line asserts three numbers, only one of which you typed:

H0=70H_0 = 70 and Ωm,0=0.3\Omega_{m,0} = 0.3 are the two you chose. astropy’s FlatLambdaCDM class does not even accept a curvature argument — it forces Ωk,0=0\Omega_{k,0}=0 by construction — so ΩΛ,0\Omega_{\Lambda,0} is not independently set, it is computed, as 1−Ωm,0−Ωk,0=0.71 - \Omega_{m,0} - \Omega_{k,0} = 0.7. Check the sum yourself and you get exactly 11, as the identity above guarantees it must.

With Ωm\Omega_m and ΩΛ\Omega_\Lambda in hand, $\eqref{eq:friedmann}$ becomes a concrete, checkable function of redshift. Using 1+z=1/a1+z = 1/a (Ch. 13) and the matter-dilution result from the previous section,

H(z)2=H02[Ωm(1+z)3+ΩΛ]H(z)^2 = H_0^2\left[\Omega_m(1+z)^3 + \Omega_\Lambda\right]

Build the right-hand side yourself from nothing but H0=70H_0=70, Ωm=0.3\Omega_m=0.3, ΩΛ=0.7\Omega_\Lambda=0.7, at z=0.5z=0.5, and you should get

in km/s/Mpc. That is not a number this guide asserts and asks you to trust — it is astropy’s own FlatLambdaCDM.H(0.5), computed independently from the metric machinery the library actually runs, and the two agree to machine precision:

The same H0H_0, Ωm\Omega_m, ΩΛ\Omega_\Lambda also fix the age of the universe — the time integral of 1/[(1+z)H(z)]1/[(1+z)H(z)] back from today to a=0a=0 — at

billion years. None of the three numbers above, nor the age, nor ρcrit,0\rho_{\mathrm{crit,0}}, ever enters the lens-modelling likelihood this guide spends Part V decoding: site/guide_src/lensing.py runs entirely in arcsec, with no distances at all, and this chapter’s whole apparatus enters this repository in exactly the three files cited above — Einstein radii from velocity dispersions, Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} and enclosed mass, and one supernova’s distance modulus. The money number γbinned(corr, low)=1.103±0.008\gamma_{\mathrm{binned}}(\text{corr, low}) = 1.103 \pm 0.008 does not know that H0=70H_0=70; it would come out identical if this repository had asserted H0=67H_0=67 instead. That scoping is worth holding onto precisely because it tells you where a wrong cosmology would and would not bite.

Connect to the repo

site/guide_src/cosmo.py:29 (source) is the one line this chapter’s whole worked example runs against: COSMO = FlatLambdaCDM(H0=70, Om0=0.3). The module’s own docstring, starting at site/guide_src/cosmo.py:5 (source), makes the same scoping argument as the paragraph above — cosmology enters this repository in exactly three places — and is the reason this guide’s cosmology Part is three chapters, not ten: that proportion is itself a finding about where to spend your attention, not an omission.

This repository never builds its own Friedmann-equation solver. All three files construct astropy.cosmology.FlatLambdaCDM; two of them call .angular_diameter_distance directly — reproductions/hsu-2025/07_classify_einstein_dimple.py:50 and reproductions/sheu-2024b/04_setup_multiplane.py:35, cited above — and the third, reproductions/sheu-2023/05_lightcurve_salt3.py:57, hands the object straight to sncosmo, which draws the supernova’s luminosity distance from it internally. What this chapter buys you is the ability to read .H, .age, .critical_density0, and .angular_diameter_distance — the four methods this chapter’s own worked example (ch14_frw_friedmann in site/guide_src/worked_examples.py) exercises directly — as physics rather than as API surface: .H(z) is $\eqref{eq:friedmann}$ evaluated at a redshift, .age(0) is that same equation integrated back to a=0a=0, and .critical_density0 is the reference density this chapter derived from H0H_0 alone. Ch. 15 is next: it turns the same COSMO object into the two distances, Dd,Ds,DdsD_{\mathrm{d}}, D_{\mathrm{s}}, D_{\mathrm{ds}}, that this repository’s lensing calculations actually consume, and into the non-additivity gotcha that bites everyone once.

Exercises

Exercise 14.1 — Dimensional analysis on the Friedmann equation

Confirm, from units alone, that 8πG3ρ\frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho in $\eqref{eq:friedmann}$ has the same units as H2H^2. You will need Newton’s constant’s units, [G]=m3kg−1s−2[G] = \text{m}^3\,\text{kg}^{-1}\,\text{s}^{-2}, and a mass density’s units, [ρ]=kgm−3[\rho] = \text{kg}\,\text{m}^{-3}.

Solution

[G][ρ]=(m3kg−1s−2)(kgm−3)=s−2[G][\rho] = \left(\text{m}^3\,\text{kg}^{-1}\,\text{s}^{-2}\right)\left(\text{kg}\,\text{m}^{-3}\right) = \text{s}^{-2}

which is exactly [H]2[H]^2, since H=ȧ/aH = \dot a/a is a rate (one over a time). The 8π/38\pi/3 is dimensionless, so it does not affect the check. The kc2/a2kc^2/a^2 term must independently carry units of s−2\text{s}^{-2} as well: [c2]=m2s−2[c^2] = \text{m}^2\text{s}^{-2}, so kk itself must carry units of inverse length squared unless aa is defined with units of length (some textbooks set a0≠1a_0 \ne 1 precisely to make kk dimensionless ±1\pm 1 or 00; this guide follows the convention a0=1a_0 = 1, in which case kk silently absorbs the missing length dimension). Either convention gives the same physics; just be consistent about which one a given equation is using.

Exercise 14.2 — Flatness is a measurement, not an identity

Explain, in a sentence or two, why Ωm+ΩΛ+Ωk=1\Omega_m + \Omega_\Lambda + \Omega_k = 1 can be stated with total confidence before a single measurement is made, while Ωk=0\Omega_k = 0 cannot.

Solution

The sum identity falls straight out of dividing the Friedmann equation by H02H_0^2 — it is true by the definitions of Ωm\Omega_m, ΩΛ\Omega_\Lambda, and Ωk\Omega_k as H02H_0^2-normalized pieces of an equation that already balances. It holds for any values those three symbols take, in any universe, flat or not. Ωk=0\Omega_k = 0 is a different kind of claim entirely: it says the actual curvature term is zero, which is a statement about which universe we are in, checkable only by measuring Ωm\Omega_m, ΩΛ\Omega_\Lambda (or H(z)H(z) directly) independently and seeing whether they leave any room for a curvature term. FlatLambdaCDM doesn’t measure this — it assumes it, by refusing to expose a curvature argument at all.

Exercise 14.3 — H(z) at a redshift this chapter didn’t show you

Using only H0=70H_0 = 70, Ωm=0.3\Omega_m = 0.3, ΩΛ=0.7\Omega_\Lambda = 0.7, and H(z)2=H02[Ωm(1+z)3+ΩΛ]H(z)^2 = H_0^2\left[\Omega_m(1+z)^3+\Omega_\Lambda\right], compute H(z=1)H(z=1) by hand. Then check your answer against astropy’s own value.

Solution

H(1)2=702[0.3⋅23+0.7]=4900×3.1=15190H(1)^2 = 70^2\left[0.3\cdot 2^3 + 0.7\right] = 4900 \times 3.1 = 15190

H(1)=15190≈123.25km/s/MpcH(1) = \sqrt{15190} \approx 123.25\ \text{km/s/Mpc}

which matches cosmo.COSMO.H(1.0) to machine precision:

Notice HH nearly doubled between z=0.5z=0.5 (91.6 km/s/Mpc, in the main text) and z=1z=1 (123.25 km/s/Mpc) — the matter term Ωm(1+z)3\Omega_m(1+z)^3 is starting to dominate over the constant ΩΛ\Omega_\Lambda term as you look back in time, exactly as ρm∝a−3\rho_m \propto a^{-3} says it must.

Exercise 14.4 — Where pressure would have to enter

This chapter’s derivation of $\eqref{eq:friedmann}$ never once used pressure, and it doesn’t need to: the equation it produces is exactly right. Where, physically, would you expect a Newtonian argument like this one to start failing if you tried to extend it to the second Friedmann equation (the one for ä\ddot a)?

Solution

Newton’s shell theorem and F=GMm/r2F=GMm/r^2 know about mass, full stop — pressure does not appear anywhere in Newtonian gravity as a source of attraction. In general relativity it does: the source of gravity is (loosely) ρ+3p/c2\rho + 3p/c^2, not ρ\rho alone, so a medium under positive pressure gravitates more, and a negative-pressure component (which is exactly what makes something behave like a cosmological constant) can drive ä\ddot a positive — accelerated expansion — with no Newtonian counterpart at all. This is the same family of “GR adds a term Newton has no room for” as the factor of two in Ch. 16, where light bends twice as far as a naive Newtonian calculation predicts. Neither this chapter nor this repository ever needs the pressure-sourced equation explicitly — dark energy is supplied as a fixed density, not derived from an equation of state — but it is worth knowing where the Newtonian trick this section leaned on would have quietly stopped working.

15. Distances that do not add, and Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}

Chapter 14 gave you one object, FlatLambdaCDM(H0=70, Om0=0.3), and the equation that makes it tick. This chapter turns that object into distances you can act on — and there turn out to be three of them, not one, because “how far away” depends on whether you mean light-travel geometry, angular size, or flux. You will derive all three from the same flat FRW metric Chapter 14 wrote down, meet the one operation on them that is silently illegal — subtracting two angular-diameter distances — and use the survivor, Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}, to reproduce this repository’s own published numbers for a real cluster lens: its critical surface density and the mass enclosed inside its Einstein radius, both computed from nothing but two redshifts and five lines of code.

What you can skip

If comoving, angular-diameter, and luminosity distance are already second nature — including the fact that they differ by explicit factors of (1+z)(1+z), not by anything mysterious — skip Three distances, one universe and go straight to D_ds != D_s - D_d. That section is not a subtle GR effect; it is an algebra trap this repository’s own code has to dodge every time it builds a lens model, and it is worth reading even if you could write down DA(z)D_{\mathrm{A}}(z) from memory. If you also already know Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}, skip straight to The Carousel, where the payoff is two real, checkable numbers.

Three distances, one universe

In a flat, static, Euclidean space “distance” needs no qualifier. In an expanding one it does, because the three operations you might use a distance for — timing a light ray, measuring an angular size, and measuring a flux — stop agreeing with each other once redshift is not tiny. This section derives the three you need, in order, each one built on the last.

Comoving distance. Ch. 14 wrote down the FRW metric; this repository only ever uses its flat (k=0k=0) case, where the radial part simplifies to ds2=−c2dt2+a(t)2[dr2+r2dΩ2]ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + a(t)^2\left[dr^2 + r^2\,d\Omega^2\right]. A photon travels on a null geodesic, ds2=0ds^2=0, and along a purely radial path (dΩ=0d\Omega=0) that forces cdt=a(t)drc\,dt = a(t)\,dr. Define the comoving distance as the coordinate distance such a photon covers:

DC(z)≡∫tet0cdta(t) D_{\mathrm{C}}(z) \;\equiv\; \int_{t_e}^{t_0} \frac{c\,dt}{a(t)}

Change the integration variable from cosmic time to redshift using Ch. 13’s a(te)=1/(1+z)a(t_e) = 1/(1+z) and Ch. 14’s H≡ȧ/aH \equiv \dot a/a: differentiating a=(1+z)−1a = (1+z)^{-1} gives da/dz=−(1+z)−2da/dz = -(1+z)^{-2}, and dt=da/ȧ=da/(aH)dt = da/\dot a = da/(aH), so dt=−dz/[(1+z)H(z)]dt = -dz/[(1+z)H(z)]. Absorbing the sign by integrating from 00 to zz instead of tet_e to t0t_0:

DC(z)=c∫0zdz′H(z′) D_{\mathrm{C}}(z) \;=\; c\int_0^z \frac{dz'}{H(z')} \label{eq:dc}

That is Ch. 14’s Friedmann equation, integrated along the line of sight. astropy performs $\eqref{eq:dc}$ numerically — there is no closed form once both Ωm\Omega_m and ΩΛ\Omega_\Lambda are nonzero — and its comoving_distance method is exactly this integral. At z=2.0z=2.0:

DC(2.0)≈5179.862Mpc D_{\mathrm{C}}(2.0) \approx 5179.862\ \mathrm{Mpc}

Angular-diameter distance. The metric’s transverse piece, a(t)2r2dΩ2a(t)^2 r^2\,d\Omega^2, is a genuine 2-sphere of physical (proper) radius a(t)ra(t)\,r at fixed tt — this is Ch. 13’s “proper distance =a(t)×=a(t)\times comoving distance” rule, now applied to the transverse direction instead of the radial one. An object of physical transverse size ℓ\ell, sitting at comoving radius rr at the moment tet_e its light was emitted, therefore subtends δθ=ℓ/[a(te)r]\delta\theta = \ell / [a(t_e)\,r] — plain Euclidean geometry on a sphere of that radius, nothing relativistic beyond the metric itself. Define DA≡ℓ/δθ=a(te)rD_{\mathrm{A}} \equiv \ell/\delta\theta = a(t_e)\,r. In a flat universe the comoving radial coordinate rr is DC(z)D_{\mathrm{C}}(z) — no curvature-dependent sin\sin or sinh\sinh correction, since this repository never leaves k=0k=0 — so, using a(te)=1/(1+z)a(t_e) = 1/(1+z):

DA(z)=DC(z)1+z D_{\mathrm{A}}(z) \;=\; \frac{D_{\mathrm{C}}(z)}{1+z} \label{eq:da}

This is astropy’s .angular_diameter_distance, and the one function this repository actually calls: cosmo.d_a at site/guide_src/cosmo.py:32 (source). At z=2.0z=2.0: DA(2.0)=DC(2.0)/3≈1726.621MpcD_{\mathrm{A}}(2.0) = D_{\mathrm{C}}(2.0)/3 \approx 1726.621\ \mathrm{Mpc}.

Luminosity distance. Put a source of luminosity LL at comoving distance DC(z)D_{\mathrm{C}}(z), radiating isotropically. By the time its light is observed it has spread over a sphere of physical area 4πDC(z)24\pi D_{\mathrm{C}}(z)^2 (using a0≡a(t0)=1a_0\equiv a(t_0)=1, today). Ordinary inverse-square dilution alone would give F=L/[4πDC(z)2]F = L/[4\pi D_{\mathrm{C}}(z)^2], but two more factors of (1+z)(1+z) cut the observed flux further: each photon’s energy is itself redshifted, Eobs=Eemit/(1+z)E_{\mathrm{obs}} = E_{\mathrm{emit}}/(1+z), and the arrival rate of photons is time-dilated by the same factor — photons emitted a proper time δte\delta t_e apart arrive spaced by δte(1+z)\delta t_e\,(1+z). Combining all three:

F=L4πDC(z)2(1+z)2 F = \frac{L}{4\pi D_{\mathrm{C}}(z)^2 (1+z)^2}

Flux is defined via F≡L/(4πDL2)F \equiv L/(4\pi D_{\mathrm{L}}^2), so matching the two expressions gives DL(z)=(1+z)DC(z)=(1+z)2DA(z)D_{\mathrm{L}}(z) = (1+z)\,D_{\mathrm{C}}(z) = (1+z)^2\,D_{\mathrm{A}}(z). At z=2.0z=2.0: DL(2.0)=9×1726.621≈15539.586MpcD_{\mathrm{L}}(2.0) = 9 \times 1726.621 \approx 15539.586\ \mathrm{Mpc}

— matching astropy’s own luminosity_distance to better than a millimeter in 15.515.5 billion parsecs:

DLD_{\mathrm{L}} is what a Type Ia supernova’s distance modulus, m−M=5log⁡10(DL/10pc)m - M = 5\log_{10}(D_{\mathrm{L}}/10\,\mathrm{pc}), actually consumes — the third and final place cosmology enters this repository, reproductions/sheu-2023/05_lightcurve_salt3.py:57 (source), a lensed-supernova campaign this guide does not otherwise follow. Everything else in this guide — every θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}}, every Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} — uses only DAD_{\mathrm{A}}, under the repository’s own subscripted names DdD_{\mathrm{d}} (to the lens), DsD_{\mathrm{s}} (to the source), and DdsD_{\mathrm{ds}} (between them) — never Ds−DdD_{\mathrm{s}}-D_{\mathrm{d}}, which is the next section’s whole point.

D_ds != D_s - D_d

State it as plainly as the notation contract this guide follows demands: DdsD_{\mathrm{ds}} is not Ds−DdD_{\mathrm{s}}-D_{\mathrm{d}}. Angular-diameter distances do not add, and the reason is entirely algebraic, not a mystery of curved spacetime — you already have every piece needed to derive it.

The general angular-diameter distance between two redshifts, in a flat universe, is

DA(z1,z2)=DC(z2)−DC(z1)1+z2 D_{\mathrm{A}}(z_1,z_2) \;=\; \frac{D_{\mathrm{C}}(z_2)-D_{\mathrm{C}}(z_1)}{1+z_2} \label{eq:dds}

— the formula astropy’s angular_diameter_distance_z1z2 evaluates for FlatLambdaCDM, and exactly what cosmo.d_ds at site/guide_src/cosmo.py:37 (source) calls. Two things about $\eqref{eq:dds}$ are worth noticing before touching a number. First, it reduces correctly at z1=0z_1=0 (Exercise 15.2 makes you check this): DA(0,z2)=DC(z2)/(1+z2)=DA(z2)D_{\mathrm{A}}(0,z_2) = D_{\mathrm{C}}(z_2)/(1+z_2) = D_{\mathrm{A}}(z_2), exactly $\eqref{eq:da}$. Second — and this is the trap — DdsD_{\mathrm{ds}} divides by (1+zs)(1+z_s) once, applied to the difference of two comoving distances. It does not divide DC(zl)D_{\mathrm{C}}(z_l) by (1+zl)(1+z_l) and DC(zs)D_{\mathrm{C}}(z_s) by (1+zs)(1+z_s) separately and then subtract. But that second, wrong operation is exactly what Ds−DdD_{\mathrm{s}}-D_{\mathrm{d}} is:

Ds−Dd=DC(zs)1+zs−DC(zl)1+zl D_{\mathrm{s}}-D_{\mathrm{d}} \;=\; \frac{D_{\mathrm{C}}(z_s)}{1+z_s} - \frac{D_{\mathrm{C}}(z_l)}{1+z_l}

You already know this

Two quantities that were each independently rescaled by a different factor do not combine correctly under subtraction — this is the same reason you cannot take two activations that were each standardized by a different layer’s own running mean and variance, subtract them, and expect the result to be meaningfully normalized. DdD_{\mathrm{d}} and DsD_{\mathrm{s}} are each already divided by their own (1+z)(1+z); the fix is to undo that per-term rescaling — work in DCD_{\mathrm{C}}, which really is additive — and apply a single, shared rescaling only at the end.

Subtracting $\eqref{eq:dds}$ and the naive expression above, the DC(zs)D_{\mathrm{C}}(z_s) terms cancel identically, leaving a closed form entirely in terms of the lens distance:

Dds−(Ds−Dd)=DC(zl)[11+zl−11+zs]=Ddzs−zl1+zs D_{\mathrm{ds}} - \left(D_{\mathrm{s}}-D_{\mathrm{d}}\right) \;=\; D_{\mathrm{C}}(z_l)\left[\frac{1}{1+z_l}-\frac{1}{1+z_s}\right] \;=\; D_{\mathrm{d}}\,\frac{z_s-z_l}{1+z_s}

(using DC(zl)=Dd(1+zl)D_{\mathrm{C}}(z_l) = D_{\mathrm{d}}(1+z_l) in the last step). Now the numbers, for zl=0.5z_l=0.5, zs=2.0z_s=2.0 — the same pair Ch. 13’s exercises already flagged as this chapter’s test case, chosen specifically because (1+z)(1+z) is nowhere near 11 for either redshift:

Dd≈1259.084Mpc,Ds≈1726.621Mpc D_{\mathrm{d}} \approx 1259.084\ \mathrm{Mpc}, \qquad D_{\mathrm{s}} \approx 1726.621\ \mathrm{Mpc}

The correct DdsD_{\mathrm{ds}}, from $\eqref{eq:dds}$ or equivalently cosmo.d_ds(0.5, 2.0):

Dds≈1097.079Mpc D_{\mathrm{ds}} \approx 1097.079\ \mathrm{Mpc}

Build it the long way, from the comoving distances directly — DC(0.5)≈1888.625D_{\mathrm{C}}(0.5)\approx1888.625 Mpc and DC(2.0)≈5179.862D_{\mathrm{C}}(2.0)\approx5179.862 Mpc, subtract, then divide once by 1+zs=31+z_s=3:

5179.862−1888.6253≈1097.079Mpc \frac{5179.862-1888.625}{3} \approx 1097.079\ \mathrm{Mpc}

and it lands on the same number to machine precision:

The naive subtraction, by contrast:

Ds−Dd≈467.537Mpc D_{\mathrm{s}}-D_{\mathrm{d}} \approx 467.537\ \mathrm{Mpc}

— less than half of DdsD_{\mathrm{ds}}, a factor of

2.34652.3465 off, silently. The closed-form gap derived above, Dd(zs−zl)/(1+zs)=1259.084×1.5/3≈629.542MpcD_{\mathrm{d}}\,(z_s-z_l)/(1+z_s) = 1259.084 \times 1.5/3 \approx 629.542\ \mathrm{Mpc}

matches the actual gap between the two numbers above exactly:

This is not a rounding error or a subtle relativistic correction to chase down — it is what happens whenever you subtract two numbers that were each divided by something different before you got them.

Sigma_crit: the natural unit of surface density

Convergence, κ≡Σ/Σcr\kappa \equiv \Sigma/\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}, is the surface mass density Σ\Sigma of a lens measured in units of a reference density Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} built entirely from cc, GG, and the three distances of the previous section:

Σcr=c24πGDsDdDds \Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} \;=\; \frac{c^2}{4\pi G}\,\frac{D_{\mathrm{s}}}{D_{\mathrm{d}}D_{\mathrm{ds}}}

Dimensional analysis alone forces this shape to be plausible before you know anything about why it is the right one: [c2/G]=(m2s−2)/(m3kg−1s−2)=kg/m[c^2/G] = (\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}})/(\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}) = \mathrm{kg/m}, and the distance ratio Ds/(DdDds)D_{\mathrm{s}}/(D_{\mathrm{d}}D_{\mathrm{ds}}) carries units m/m2=m−1\mathrm m/\mathrm m^2 = \mathrm m^{-1}, so the product is kg/m2\mathrm{kg/m^2} — a surface density, exactly as the name promises. Dimensional analysis cannot tell you why this particular combination of distances is the physically correct one, only that whatever the correct formula turns out to be, it had better have this shape — the actual physics (the point-mass deflection law and the geometry of a lens, source, and observer in a line) is Ch. 16–Ch. 17’s job, and the fact that κ=1\kappa=1 marks the boundary between one image and several is Ch. 19’s. What matters here is narrower: Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} is a well-defined, computable number the moment you have DdD_{\mathrm{d}}, DsD_{\mathrm{s}}, and DdsD_{\mathrm{ds}} in hand, and — because DdsD_{\mathrm{ds}} appears in the denominator — it inherits the previous section’s non-additivity trap directly: get DdsD_{\mathrm{ds}} wrong by a factor of 2.32.3 and Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}, and every mass this guide will ever quote, is wrong by the same factor.

The Carousel: reproducing the repo’s own numbers

The Carousel Lens (Sheu et al. 2024, reproductions/sheu-2024b/README.md) is a cluster-scale strong lens at zl=0.49z_l=0.49, with its Einstein radius quoted relative to one of five spectroscopically-confirmed source planes, zs=1.432z_s=1.432: θE=13.03″\theta_{\mathrm{E}}=13.03'' for the primary deflector. Plug those two redshifts into Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}:

Σcr(0.49,1.432)≈2.376×1015M⊙/Mpc2 \Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}(0.49,\,1.432) \;\approx\; 2.376\times10^{15}\ M_\odot/\mathrm{Mpc}^2

— equivalently 2376.07M⊙/pc22376.07\ M_\odot/\mathrm{pc}^2

which is reproductions/sheu-2024b/04_setup_multiplane.py:128 (source) computed independently and, per that script’s own printed output (f"{sigma_crit:.3e}"), to four significant figures.

To turn θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}} into a physical size you need one more conversion: how much proper transverse distance one arcsecond spans at zl=0.49z_l=0.49, which is DdD_{\mathrm{d}} itself times 1″1'' in radians — Ch. 9’s 206264.8206264.8 factor, applied here to a cosmological rather than a local distance:

1″×Dd(0.49)≈6.038×10−3Mpc 1'' \times D_{\mathrm{d}}(0.49) \;\approx\; 6.038\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{Mpc}

so ℓE=6.038×10−3×13.03≈0.07868Mpc=78.68\ell_{\mathrm{E}} = 6.038\times10^{-3}\times 13.03 \approx 0.07868\ \mathrm{Mpc} = 78.68 kpc

and, taking M(<θE)=ΣcrπℓE2M(<\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) = \Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}\,\pi \ell_{\mathrm{E}}^2 on faith for now (why this particular formula gives the enclosed mass regardless of the density profile’s shape is Ch. 19’s identity):

M(<θE)≈4.621×1013M⊙ M(<\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) \;\approx\; 4.621\times10^{13}\ M_\odot

Sheu et al. (2024)’s own Table 2 quotes M(<θE)=4.78×1013M⊙M(<\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) = 4.78\times10^{13}\ M_\odot for this deflector — this chapter’s from-scratch, geometry-only estimate lands 3.3%3.3\% low:

Not a bug. The formula used here assumes a perfectly circular lens (mean κ=1\kappa=1 inside a circle of radius θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}}); the published figure comes from the paper’s full elliptical mass model, and the primary deflector’s axis ratio is q=0.87q=0.87 — close to circular but not exactly. A small, well-understood correction, and Exercise 15.3 asks you to check that its size moves in the direction the ellipticity story predicts once you apply the identical method to the Carousel’s more elongated second deflector.

Connect to the repo

Every distance in this chapter is one of five short functions in site/guide_src/cosmo.py (source): d_a (cosmo.py:32) wraps .angular_diameter_distance for $\eqref{eq:da}$; d_ds (cosmo.py:37) wraps .angular_diameter_distance_z1z2 for $\eqref{eq:dds}$ and is annotated, in its own docstring, with exactly this chapter’s warning — never a subtraction; sigma_crit (cosmo.py:45) is Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} verbatim; arcsec_to_mpc (cosmo.py:61) is the 1″×Dd1''\times D_{\mathrm{d}} conversion behind ℓE\ell_{\mathrm{E}}; and mass_within_theta_e (cosmo.py:66) is the whole Carousel worked example in four lines. site/guide_src/worked_examples.py’s ch15_distances_and_sigma_crit reproduces reproductions/sheu-2024b/04_setup_multiplane.py:125–131 (source) line for line, against the published Table 2 numbers printed at that script’s own :135–138.

Ch. 13 and Ch. 14 already made the scoping argument this chapter’s numbers confirm from the distance side: reproductions/claude-giga-lens/cgl/ never imports astropy.cosmology at all, so none of DdD_{\mathrm{d}}, DsD_{\mathrm{s}}, DdsD_{\mathrm{ds}}, or Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} enters the money-number pipeline. This repository’s two remaining cosmology campaigns need nothing else this chapter didn’t already derive: reproductions/hsu-2025/07_classify_einstein_dimple.py:114–116 (source) uses DsD_{\mathrm{s}} and DdsD_{\mathrm{ds}} to turn a velocity dispersion into an Einstein radius, derived in full in Ch. 19; and reproductions/sheu-2023/05_lightcurve_salt3.py:57 uses DLD_{\mathrm{L}}, this chapter’s third distance, for a lensed supernova’s magnitude — the one place in this repository a distance sets a brightness rather than a length or an angle.

Exercises

Exercise 15.1 — Comoving distance at low redshift

Chapter 13 derived the linear Hubble law, v≈H0dv \approx H_0 d, valid for z≪1z \ll 1. Show that the comoving-distance integral $\eqref{eq:dc}$ reduces to this law in the same limit, and that DA(z)≈DC(z)D_{\mathrm{A}}(z)\approx D_{\mathrm{C}}(z) there too. (You need only that H(z′)→H0H(z')\to H_0 as z′→0z'\to0 — not Ωm\Omega_m or ΩΛ\Omega_\Lambda individually.)

Solution

For z≪1z\ll1, H(z′)H(z') barely moves from H0H_0 across the whole integration range [0,z][0,z] in $\eqref{eq:dc}$, so to leading order it can be pulled outside the integral: DC(z)≈c∫0zdz′/H0=cz/H0D_{\mathrm{C}}(z)\approx c\int_0^z dz'/H_0 = cz/H_0 — exactly the linear Hubble law solved for distance, d=v/H0d = v/H_0 with v≈czv\approx cz. And since DA=DC/(1+z)D_{\mathrm{A}}=D_{\mathrm{C}}/(1+z), at z≪1z\ll1 the factor (1+z)≈1(1+z)\approx1 to first order, so DA(z)≈DC(z)D_{\mathrm{A}}(z)\approx D_{\mathrm{C}}(z) as well — all three distances of this chapter agree in the nearby universe (since DL=(1+z)2DAD_{\mathrm{L}}=(1+z)^2D_{\mathrm{A}} collapses to the same limit too). They only pull apart once (1+z)(1+z) stops being close to 11, which is exactly why this chapter’s worked example uses zl=0.5z_l=0.5, zs=2.0z_s=2.0 rather than anything small.

Exercise 15.2 — The two-redshift formula, checked at its own boundary

Show that $\eqref{eq:dds}$, DA(z1,z2)=[DC(z2)−DC(z1)]/(1+z2)D_{\mathrm{A}}(z_1,z_2) = [D_{\mathrm{C}}(z_2)-D_{\mathrm{C}}(z_1)]/(1+z_2), reduces correctly to the single-redshift formula $\eqref{eq:da}$ when z1=0z_1=0, and explain in one sentence why that check has to pass.

Solution

Set z1=0z_1=0: DC(0)=0D_{\mathrm{C}}(0)=0 trivially — there is no distance to travel to reach redshift zero, since that is here — so DA(0,z2)=DC(z2)/(1+z2)D_{\mathrm{A}}(0,z_2) = D_{\mathrm{C}}(z_2)/(1+z_2), exactly $\eqref{eq:da}$. It has to pass because DA(0,z)D_{\mathrm{A}}(0,z) and “the angular-diameter distance to zz” are not two different quantities that happen to agree — they are the same quantity under two names, an observer at redshift zero looking out to zz. A two-redshift formula that failed this check would be wrong for every pair of redshifts, not just the edge case z1=0z_1=0.

Exercise 15.3 — The Carousel’s other deflector

The Carousel’s own Table 2 lists a second deflector, Ld, with θE=0.99″\theta_{\mathrm{E}}=0.99'' (also quoted relative to zs=1.432z_s=1.432) and a more elongated shape than the primary — axis ratio q=0.69q=0.69, versus 0.870.87 for the primary. Using the same Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} already computed for this system, compute M(<θE)M(<\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) for Ld and compare it to the paper’s published 2.77×1011M⊙2.77\times10^{11}\ M_\odot.

Solution

Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} depends only on the redshifts, which are unchanged (both deflectors sit at zl=0.49z_l=0.49, both θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}} values are quoted relative to the same zs=1.432z_s=1.432), so only ℓE\ell_{\mathrm{E}} changes: ℓE,Ld=6.038×10−3×0.99≈5.978×10−3Mpc\ell_{\mathrm{E},\mathrm{Ld}} = 6.038\times10^{-3}\times0.99 \approx 5.978\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{Mpc}. Then M(<θE)=ΣcrπℓE,Ld2≈2.668×1011M⊙M(<\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) = \Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}\,\pi \ell_{\mathrm{E},\mathrm{Ld}}^2 \approx 2.668\times10^{11}\ M_\odot against the paper’s 2.77×10112.77\times10^{11}: a ratio of 0.9630.963 — a slightly larger shortfall than the primary deflector’s 3.3%3.3\%. That is exactly the direction the ellipticity story predicts: Ld’s axis ratio (q=0.69q=0.69) is farther from circular than the primary’s (q=0.87q=0.87), so the circular-equivalent approximation this chapter’s formula makes should miss by more, not less. It does.

Exercise 15.4 — Dimensional analysis of Sigma_crit

Confirm, from units alone, that c24πGDsDdDds\dfrac{c^2}{4\pi G}\dfrac{D_{\mathrm{s}}}{D_{\mathrm{d}}D_{\mathrm{ds}}} has units of mass per area, using [c]=m/s[c]=\mathrm{m/s}, [G]=m3kg−1s−2[G]=\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}, and [D]=m[D]=\mathrm{m}.

Solution

[c2/G]=m2s−2m3kg−1s−2=kgm[c^2/G] = \dfrac{\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}}{\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}}. The distance ratio Ds/(DdDds)D_{\mathrm{s}}/(D_{\mathrm{d}}D_{\mathrm{ds}}) carries units m/m2=m−1\mathrm m/\mathrm m^2 = \mathrm m^{-1}. Multiplying: kgm×1m=kgm2\dfrac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm m}\times\dfrac1{\mathrm m} = \dfrac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm m^2} — mass per area, exactly a surface density; 4π4\pi is dimensionless and does not affect the check. This argument alone cannot tell you why this particular combination of cc, GG, and three distances is the physically relevant one — only that whatever the correct formula turns out to be, it had better have this shape, because nothing else built from cc, GG, and three lengths has the right units to be a surface density at all.

16. How much light bends, and the factor of two

This chapter buys you the right to treat every galaxy in this repository as a flat sheet of surface density Σ(𝛉)\Sigma(\boldsymbol\theta), and every deflection as the gradient of a 2-D potential — the machinery Ch. 17 onward runs without re-justifying it. It earns that right by settling, from first principles, a question that took Einstein two tries: exactly how far a ray of light bends past a mass, and why general relativity’s answer is exactly twice the naive Newtonian one, not some approximate correction. Get that factor of two wrong and Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}, κ\kappa, and θE\theta_{\mathrm E} would all be off by it two chapters from now — everything from Ch. 17’s lens equation to the γbinned=1.103\gamma_{\mathrm{binned}}=1.103 money number this book is chasing rests on this one multiplicative constant being right.

What you can skip

If you already know the GR light-bending result and where the factor of two comes from, skip Newtonian deflection and The factor of two and start at The thin-lens approximation — that section is the one piece of new machinery every later chapter leans on: it is where Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} (Ch. 15) and ψ\psi (Ch. 6) actually meet. If you’re already comfortable treating a lens as a flat projected sheet with no further justification needed, skip straight to Connect to the repo. Nothing in this chapter touches γ\gamma — the density-slope parameter does not exist until Ch. 20; this one is about the coupling constant GG, not the slope.

Newtonian deflection

Set up the calculation an 18th-century Newtonian would recognize: a point mass MM sits at the origin, and something travels past it in a straight line (undeflected, to leading order — an impulse approximation is self-consistent exactly as long as the true deflection turns out to be small) at speed cc, offset by an impact parameter bb. Parametrize position along the path by x=ctx=ct, so the distance to the mass at any moment is r=b2+x2r=\sqrt{b^2+x^2}.

Newtonian gravity pulls with acceleration GM/r2GM/r^2 directed toward the mass. Only the component perpendicular to the direction of travel actually bends the path; by similar triangles that component is b/rb/r of the total:

a⟂(x)=GMr2⋅br=GMb(b2+x2)3/2. a_\perp(x) = \frac{GM}{r^2}\cdot\frac{b}{r} = \frac{GMb}{(b^2+x^2)^{3/2}}.

Gravitational acceleration does not depend on the falling body’s own mass — Galileo’s observation, built into Newtonian gravity as the equality of inertial and gravitational mass — so this formula holds for a cannonball, a comet, or (in the 18th-century corpuscular picture) a particle of light, provided it moves at cc. Integrate the perpendicular acceleration over the whole encounter to get the sideways velocity picked up:

Δv⟂=∫−∞∞a⟂dt=GMbc∫−∞∞dx(b2+x2)3/2. \Delta v_\perp = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} a_\perp\,dt = \frac{GMb}{c}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{(b^2+x^2)^{3/2}}.

The integral is elementary — differentiate x/(b2b2+x2)x/(b^2\sqrt{b^2+x^2}) and check it reproduces the integrand, or substitute x=btan⁡ux=b\tan u — and comes out to 2/b22/b^2 regardless of method:

∫−∞∞dx(b2+x2)3/2=[xb2b2+x2]−∞∞=2b2. \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{(b^2+x^2)^{3/2}} = \left[\frac{x}{b^2\sqrt{b^2+x^2}}\right]_{-\infty}^{\infty} = \frac{2}{b^2}.

So Δv⟂=2GM/(cb)\Delta v_\perp = 2GM/(cb). For a small deflection the bend angle is just the ratio of the sideways kick to the forward speed, α≈Δv⟂/c\alpha\approx\Delta v_\perp/c:

αN=2GMc2b. \alpha_{\mathrm N} = \frac{2GM}{c^2 b}. \label{eq:newton-deflection}

This is precisely the calculation Henry Cavendish worked out privately around 1784 and Johann Georg von Soldner published in 1801, more than a century before anyone had heard of relativity — nothing here used anything but F=GMm/r2F=GMm/r^2 and a photon treated as an ordinary, if massless, projectile.

The factor of two

Einstein’s own first attempt, in 1911, used only the equivalence principle — the same mass-independence this chapter’s derivation leaned on — applied to how a gravitational potential affects the local speed of light, rather than to a Newtonian force directly. That calculation reproduced $\eqref{eq:newton-deflection}$ almost exactly: two conceptually different arguments, 127 years apart, landing on the same number, because the equivalence-principle argument (in the weak-field limit) only sees the part of spacetime’s geometry that a slow-moving Newtonian projectile would also see — the warping of time.

The completed field equations of 1915 add a second ingredient with no Newtonian counterpart at all: mass also curves space, not only the flow of time through it. In the weak-field limit the metric splits cleanly into these two pieces,

ds2=−(1+2Φc2)c2dt2+(1−2Φc2)(dx2+dy2+dz2),Φ=−GMr, ds^2 = -\left(1+\frac{2\Phi}{c^2}\right)c^2\,dt^2 + \left(1-\frac{2\Phi}{c^2}\right)\left(dx^2+dy^2+dz^2\right), \qquad \Phi=-\frac{GM}{r},

and a full derivation — which needs the null-geodesic equation, genuine tensor calculus this guide skips — shows the two terms contribute equally to the bending of anything moving at v=cv=c. A slow-moving object weights the spatial term by a factor of order (v/c)2(v/c)^2 and barely notices it, which is exactly why $\eqref{eq:newton-deflection}$’s ordinary Newtonian mechanics, built for slow particles, only ever captured the time half. Light has no such suppression, and the result is exact, not an approximate correction on top of Newton:

αGR=4GMc2b=2αN. \alpha_{\mathrm{GR}} = \frac{4GM}{c^2 b} = 2\,\alpha_{\mathrm N}. \label{eq:gr-deflection}

Worked check: starlight grazing the Sun. Put M=M⊙M=M_\odot and b=R⊙b=R_\odot — light skimming the visible edge of the Sun, the only geometry an eclipse lets you test from the ground, since otherwise the Sun’s own glare drowns out any star close enough on the sky to show a measurable bend. GM⊙/c2≈1476.6GM_\odot/c^2\approx1476.6 m — exactly half the Sun’s own Schwarzschild radius, 2.9532.953 km , a number with no other role in this calculation beyond being a memorable way to carry GM⊙/c2GM_\odot/c^2 around. Divide by R⊙=6.957×108R_\odot=6.957\times10^8 m and convert radians to arcsec with the 206265206265 factor Ch. 9 built:

αN=2×1476.6m6.957×108m×206265″≈0.876″. \alpha_{\mathrm N} = \frac{2\times1476.6\ \text{m}}{6.957\times10^8\ \text{m}} \times 206265'' \approx 0.876''.

αGR=2αN≈1.751″. \alpha_{\mathrm{GR}} = 2\,\alpha_{\mathrm N} \approx 1.751''.

The ratio is exactly 22 — nothing in $\eqref{eq:newton-deflection}$ and $\eqref{eq:gr-deflection}$ lets it be anything else, since αGR\alpha_{\mathrm{GR}} was defined as double αN\alpha_{\mathrm N} above. The physics is in which of the two numbers, 0.876″0.876'' or 1.751″1.751'', the sky actually shows.

That question is what the Astronomer Royal Frank Dyson organized twin expeditions to answer during the total solar eclipse of May 29, 1919 — Arthur Eddington to Príncipe, Andrew Crommelin and Charles Davidson to Sobral — a total eclipse being the only moment starlight near the Sun’s limb is visible at all. Three numbers were on the table going in: 0″0'' (no deflection, Newton’s first-approximation intuition that a massless particle isn’t pulled by gravity at all), 0.876″0.876'' (Cavendish/Soldner’s Newtonian corpuscular estimate, matching Einstein’s own incomplete 1911 result), and 1.751″1.751'' (the full 1915 theory). Dyson, Eddington, and Davidson’s 1920 paper reported results close to the GR prediction and clearly separated from the Newtonian one, and the announcement made Einstein a worldwide public figure within days.

You already know this

A well-designed experiment does not just confirm a model — it discriminates between models that make distinct, numeric predictions. Eddington’s eclipse had three sharply separated candidates to rule between: 0″0'', 0.876″0.876'', and 1.751″1.751''. That is exactly the shape of the test this repository runs on its own money number in Ch. 25: not “is there a signal,” but “which of several numerically distinct values does the data actually prefer” — and, as with Eddington’s data, the answer there turns out to be less clean than a single confirmed number.

The thin-lens approximation

A real galaxy is not a point mass; it is a 3-D distribution of stars and dark matter with genuine depth along the line of sight. Superposing $\eqref{eq:gr-deflection}$ over every mass element in that distribution, and justifying the step where a 3-D galaxy collapses to a flat 2-D sheet, is what Ch. 6 forward-referenced as this chapter’s job.

Start from the Newtonian potential Φ\Phi sourced by the lens’s 3-D density ρ\rho, which obeys ∇2Φ=4πGρ\nabla^2\Phi=4\pi G\rho (Ch. 6’s Poisson equation, one dimension up — the same divergence-theorem argument, sourced by mass instead of a unit point charge). Pick a line of sight at fixed transverse physical position 𝛏\boldsymbol\xi and let zz run along it. Split the 3-D Laplacian into a transverse piece and a zz piece, ∇2Φ=∇⟂2Φ+∂2Φ/∂z2\nabla^2\Phi = \nabla^2_\perp\Phi + \partial^2\Phi/\partial z^2, and integrate the whole equation along zz:

∫−∞∞∇⟂2Φdz=4πG∫−∞∞ρdz−[∂Φ∂z]−∞∞. \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\nabla^2_\perp\Phi\,dz = 4\pi G\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\rho\,dz - \left[\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial z}\right]_{-\infty}^{\infty}.

The boundary term vanishes because Φ→const\Phi\to\text{const} far outside any finite mass distribution, so its slope does too. What survives is an exact identity — no thinness assumed anywhere yet:

∫−∞∞∇⟂2Φdz=4πGΣ(𝛏),Σ(𝛏)≡∫−∞∞ρdz. \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\nabla_\perp^2\Phi\,dz = 4\pi G\,\Sigma(\boldsymbol\xi), \qquad \Sigma(\boldsymbol\xi)\equiv\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\rho\,dz. \label{eq:projected-poisson}

Σ\Sigma is the same line-of-sight projection Ch. 3 built for a spherical ρ∼r−γ\rho\sim r^{-\gamma}; here it is the identical operation — integrate the density straight down the line of sight — applied to whatever shape the galaxy actually has.

Where “thin” actually enters. $\eqref{eq:projected-poisson}$ needed no approximation. The approximation is in what comes next: treating every mass element as sitting at one shared angular-diameter distance DdD_{\mathrm d}, rather than at its own true distance Dd+zD_{\mathrm d}+z depending on where along the line of sight it happens to be. That is valid exactly when the galaxy’s own line-of-sight depth is negligible next to DdD_{\mathrm d} itself. A giant elliptical is a few to a few tens of kiloparsecs across; a fiducial lens at zl=0.5z_{\mathrm l}=0.5 (the same system Ch. 10 and Ch. 19 use) sits at Dd≈1259D_{\mathrm d}\approx1259 Mpc . A 1010-kpc depth against that distance is a ratio of about 8×10−68\times10^{-6} — eight parts in a million. That number, not any statement about a galaxy being “flat,” is the actual license to write Σ(𝛉)\Sigma(\boldsymbol\theta) as living on a single plane at a single distance.

With the lens confined to one plane, convert to the angular coordinate 𝛉=𝛏/Dd\boldsymbol\theta=\boldsymbol\xi/D_{\mathrm d} and define the lensing potential, absorbing the distance ratios and the GR normalization from the previous section into one object:

ψ(𝛉)≡DdsDdDs⋅2c2∫−∞∞Φ(Dd𝛉,z)dz. \psi(\boldsymbol\theta) \equiv \frac{D_{\mathrm{ds}}}{D_{\mathrm d}D_{\mathrm s}} \cdot\frac{2}{c^2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\Phi(D_{\mathrm d}\boldsymbol\theta,z)\,dz. \label{eq:psi-projection}

(DdsD_{\mathrm{ds}} here is the distance between the lens and source redshifts, never Ds−DdD_{\mathrm s}-D_{\mathrm d} — Ch. 15 is the reminder to keep repeating.) The 2/c22/c^2 is not a free normalization choice: it is $\eqref{eq:gr-deflection}$’s factor of two, carried through. Had the previous section’s naive equivalence-principle result been the whole truth, this prefactor would read 1/c21/c^2, not 2/c22/c^2 — and, as Exercise 16.4 works out exactly, everything downstream would silently be off by a factor of 22 in κ\kappa.

Now differentiate $\eqref{eq:psi-projection}$. Since 𝛏=Dd𝛉\boldsymbol\xi=D_{\mathrm d}\boldsymbol\theta is a uniform rescaling, the chain rule gives ∇θ2=Dd2∇⟂2\nabla^2_\theta = D_{\mathrm d}^2\,\nabla^2_\perp — the same conjugation rule Exercise 6.1 used for a rotation matrix, here for a uniform scale factor instead. Applying that and $\eqref{eq:projected-poisson}$:

∇θ2ψ=DdsDdDs⋅2c2⋅Dd2⋅4πGΣ(𝛉)=8πGDdDdsc2DsΣ(𝛉). \nabla^2_\theta\psi = \frac{D_{\mathrm{ds}}}{D_{\mathrm d}D_{\mathrm s}} \cdot\frac{2}{c^2}\cdot D_{\mathrm d}^2\cdot 4\pi G\,\Sigma(\boldsymbol\theta) = \frac{8\pi G\,D_{\mathrm d}D_{\mathrm{ds}}}{c^2 D_{\mathrm s}}\,\Sigma(\boldsymbol\theta).

Recognize the prefactor using Ch. 15’s Σcr=c2Ds/(4πGDdDds)\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} = c^2D_{\mathrm s}/(4\pi G D_{\mathrm d}D_{\mathrm{ds}}), so 1/Σcr=4πGDdDds/(c2Ds)1/\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} = 4\pi G D_{\mathrm d}D_{\mathrm{ds}}/(c^2D_{\mathrm s}), and the prefactor above is exactly twice that:

∇θ2ψ=2Σ(𝛉)Σcr=2κ(𝛉). \nabla^2_\theta\psi = \frac{2\,\Sigma(\boldsymbol\theta)}{\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}} = 2\kappa(\boldsymbol\theta). \label{eq:poisson-projected}

This is Ch. 6’s ∇2ψ=2κ\nabla^2\psi=2\kappa again, this time earned from an actual line-of-sight integral over real mass rather than from an abstract trace-of-Hessian argument — the two derivations meeting from opposite directions is the check that both are internally consistent.

Two unrelated 2’s, reconciled, not contradicted. Ch. 6 flagged ∇2ψ=2κ\nabla^2\psi=2\kappa’s “2” as pure convention — the trace of a 2×22\times2 identity matrix, true by the definitions of κ\kappa and Γ\Gamma as the isotropic and traceless parts of the Hessian of ψ\psi, for any physical theory of gravity you plugged into ψ\psi. That claim survives this section intact: nothing about $\eqref{eq:poisson-projected}$’s derivation used GR specifically — swap $\eqref{eq:psi-projection}$’s 2/c22/c^2 for a different constant and the same trace algebra still forces ∇2ψ=2κ\nabla^2\psi=2\kappa, just with κ\kappa meaning something else. The GR-specific fact lives one level down, in which prefactor $\eqref{eq:psi-projection}$ is entitled to use — the 22 inherited from $\eqref{eq:gr-deflection}$, not the trace’s 22. They are still two unrelated 2’s, exactly as Ch. 6 said; this section only shows precisely where each one enters the same formula.

One loose end, honestly flagged rather than swept past: for a genuine point mass, Φ=−GM/r\Phi=-GM/r makes the raw integral ∫Φdz\int\Phi\,dz in $\eqref{eq:psi-projection}$ diverge logarithmically as z→±∞z\to\pm\infty — an idealized point mass has infinite reach along every line of sight. ψ\psi itself is only ever needed through its gradient 𝛂=∇ψ\boldsymbol\alpha=\nabla\psi (Ch. 6’s point-mass check used the form θE2ln⁡r\theta_{\mathrm E}^2\ln r for exactly this reason), and that gradient is perfectly finite even where ψ\psi needs an arbitrary additive constant to be well defined. It is also why gigalens’s production EPL profile, cited in Ch. 6, hands you a closed-form 𝛂\boldsymbol\alpha directly and never constructs ψ\psi at all.

Connect to the repo

site/guide_src/lensing.py:9-19 (source) states the payoff of this whole chapter as a module-docstring bullet: “Angles in arcsec throughout. The lens-modeling likelihood in this repo is entirely angular — no cosmology enters it.” That sentence is only true because GG, cc, and MM were absorbed once, here, into Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} and the profile normalizations — never to be typed again in a per-galaxy fit. site/guide_src/cosmo.py:1-19 (source) names the three files where that absorption is undone and cosmology briefly becomes real again; site/guide_src/cosmo.py:45 (source) is this chapter’s Σcr=c2Ds/(4πGDdDds)\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}=c^2D_{\mathrm s}/(4\pi G D_{\mathrm d}D_{\mathrm{ds}}), written as code. reproductions/sheu-2024b/04_setup_multiplane.py:128 (source) is the identical formula computed inside a real campaign, for the Carousel cluster lens — the same line cosmo.sigma_crit reproduces to five significant figures in Ch. 15.

None of GG, cc, or MM survives past this chapter as an explicit constant in this repository’s own code: gigalens’s EPL and SIE deflection fields (Ch. 20) are written entirely in θE\theta_{\mathrm E}, qq, ϕ\phi, and γ\gamma — the coupling constant this chapter spent its whole length pinning down never appears in them by name again.

Exercises

Exercise 16.1 — Dimensional check on 2GM/(c2b)2GM/(c^2b)

Confirm from units alone that 2GM/(c2b)2GM/(c^2b) is dimensionless (an angle, in radians), using [G]=m3kg−1s−2[G]=\text{m}^3\,\text{kg}^{-1}\,\text{s}^{-2}, [M]=kg[M]=\text{kg}, [c]=ms−1[c]=\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}, [b]=m[b]=\text{m}.

Solution

[G][M][c]2[b]=m3kg−1s−2⋅kg(m2s−2)⋅m=m3s−2m3s−2=1. \frac{[G][M]}{[c]^2[b]} = \frac{\text{m}^3\,\text{kg}^{-1}\,\text{s}^{-2}\cdot\text{kg}} {(\text{m}^2\,\text{s}^{-2})\cdot\text{m}} = \frac{\text{m}^3\,\text{s}^{-2}}{\text{m}^3\,\text{s}^{-2}} = 1.

Dimensionless, as an angle in radians has to be — the factor of 22 is a pure number and does not affect the check. The same units argument applies unchanged to $\eqref{eq:gr-deflection}$’s 44.

Exercise 16.2 — Redo the derivation for a slower projectile

Newtonian deflection assumed the passing object moves at cc. Redo the same impulse-approximation integral for something moving at a general speed vv (a comet, say, not a photon), and show the deflection angle generalizes to α=2GM/(v2b)\alpha=2GM/(v^2b). What does this say about how strongly a slow-moving object is deflected, compared to light, at the same impact parameter?

Solution

Parametrize the path by x=vtx=vt instead of x=ctx=ct. The perpendicular acceleration a⟂(x)a_\perp(x) is unchanged (it never depended on the passing object’s speed), but dt=dx/vdt=dx/v now, so

Δv⟂=GMbv∫−∞∞dx(b2+x2)3/2=2GMvb, \Delta v_\perp = \frac{GMb}{v}\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{dx}{(b^2+x^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{2GM}{vb},

and the deflection angle is Δv⟂/v=2GM/(v2b)\Delta v_\perp/v = 2GM/(v^2b) — set v=cv=c to recover $\eqref{eq:newton-deflection}$. Because this scales as 1/v21/v^2, a slower object is deflected more by the same mass at the same impact parameter, not less — light, moving at the fastest possible speed, is the least bent per unit GM/bGM/b of anything that could pass by. A slow-moving spacecraft skimming the Sun at, say, 3030 km/s would swing through a far larger angle than a photon at the same distance ever does; it is only because cc is so large that αN\alpha_{\mathrm N} comes out as a fraction of an arcsecond at all.

Exercise 16.3 — Which part of ‘thin lens’ is exact, and which is approximate

The thin-lens approximation derived $\eqref{eq:projected-poisson}$, ∫∇⟂2Φdz=4πGΣ(𝛏)\int\nabla_\perp^2\Phi\,dz=4\pi G\Sigma(\boldsymbol\xi), without ever assuming the lens is thin. Where, precisely, did an approximation get made — and what physical quantity would have to be small for it to be justified?

Solution

$\eqref{eq:projected-poisson}$ itself is exact: it needs only that Φ\Phi (and its zz-derivative) go to a constant far outside the mass distribution, which is true for any finite lens regardless of its depth. The approximation is the step right after — treating every mass element along the line of sight as sitting at the same angular-diameter distance DdD_{\mathrm d}, so that a single number DdD_{\mathrm d} (and hence a single Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}) can be used for the whole galaxy. That is justified when the galaxy’s own line-of-sight depth is tiny compared to DdD_{\mathrm d} — the ∼8×10−6\sim8\times10^{-6} ratio computed in the text — not by any property of the projection integral itself. A cluster-scale lens with several distinct mass clumps spread over hundreds of Mpc along the line of sight (a genuine multi-plane lens) is exactly the regime where this second approximation, not the first, starts to fail.

Exercise 16.4 — What would happen to κ\kappa under the wrong theory of gravity

Suppose ψnaive(𝛉)\psi_{\mathrm{naive}}(\boldsymbol\theta) used $\eqref{eq:psi-projection}$’s formula with 1/c21/c^2 in place of 2/c22/c^2 — i.e., only the incomplete 1911 equivalence-principle deflection, never doubled by the 1915 field equations. Using the same Σcr=c2Ds/(4πGDdDds)\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}=c^2D_{\mathrm s}/(4\pi GD_{\mathrm d}D_{\mathrm{ds}}) formula from Ch. 15, what would ∇θ2ψnaive\nabla^2_\theta\psi_{\mathrm{naive}} come out to, in terms of the true κ=Σ/Σcr\kappa=\Sigma/\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}?

Solution

Repeat the derivation with 1/c21/c^2 instead of 2/c22/c^2: every step is identical except the prefactor is now half of what it was, so

∇θ2ψnaive=4πGDdDdsc2DsΣ(𝛉)=Σ(𝛉)Σcr=κ(𝛉), \nabla^2_\theta\psi_{\mathrm{naive}} = \frac{4\pi G\,D_{\mathrm d}D_{\mathrm{ds}}}{c^2D_{\mathrm s}}\,\Sigma(\boldsymbol\theta) = \frac{\Sigma(\boldsymbol\theta)}{\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}} = \kappa(\boldsymbol\theta),

not 2κ2\kappa. But Ch. 6’s trace identity says the quantity anyone would call “κ\kappa” from ψnaive\psi_{\mathrm{naive}} — half the trace of its Hessian, by definition — must still satisfy ∇2ψnaive=2κnaive\nabla^2\psi_{\mathrm{naive}}=2\kappa_{\mathrm{naive}} regardless. Comparing the two expressions, κnaive=Σ/(2Σcr)=12κ\kappa_{\mathrm{naive}}=\Sigma/(2\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}) = \tfrac12\kappa: using the correct Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} formula with the wrong (undoubled) light-bending physics would make κ\kappa read at exactly half strength for the same real mass. Since the Einstein radius is defined by mean κ=1\kappa=1 (Ch. 19), a universe that bent light the Newtonian amount would need to enclose roughly twice the projected mass before calling a radius “Einstein” — the single factor of two from The factor of two propagating, unaltered, all the way to a number every strong-lensing paper quotes in its abstract.

17. The lens equation: β=θ−α\beta = \theta - \alpha

Chapter 16 established that mass bends light and by how much. This chapter turns that fact into a single equation you can actually solve, and asks the question a bent-light fact alone doesn’t answer: given a source at one position, how many images does an observer see, and where? The answer falls out of nothing more than asking how many roots a (generally nonlinear) equation has — which is why a lens can show one image, two, four, or a full ring, and why that number is not a free choice of the mass distribution but a consequence you can derive. By the end of this chapter you will have solved the equation this repository’s own renderer never has to solve, and you will know exactly why it doesn’t have to.

What you can skip

You already know that a nonlinear equation can have zero, one, or several roots, and that finding every root of g(θ)=cg(\theta)=c is a fundamentally different (and often harder) task than evaluating gg once. Skip any refresher on “root-finding is a search, not algebra.” What is not boilerplate: the specific physical content packed into 𝛂\boldsymbol\alpha (the distance-ratio scaling that erases cosmology from its shape, Chapter 16’s payoff, cashed in here), the singular isothermal sphere’s own doubles-versus-singles rule (worth deriving once by hand — it is not the “always two images” folklore you may have half-remembered), and why gigalens’s own image renderer never actually inverts the equation this chapter is named after (“Connect to the repo”).

The lens equation

Chapter 16 derived the physical bend angle 𝛂̂\hat{\boldsymbol\alpha} that a mass produces in general relativity, and the thin-lens approximation that lets a real, extended 3-D mass be treated as a single deflection evaluated at one plane (Ch. 16). Folding in the angular-diameter distances that convert a physical bend angle into an angular one produces a scaled (or “reduced”) deflection,

𝛂(𝛉)≡DdsDs𝛂̂(Dd𝛉), \boldsymbol\alpha(\boldsymbol\theta) \;\equiv\; \frac{D_{\mathrm{ds}}}{D_{\mathrm s}}\, \hat{\boldsymbol\alpha}\bigl(D_{\mathrm d}\boldsymbol\theta\bigr),

where DdsD_{\mathrm{ds}} is the lens-to-source angular diameter distance — not Ds−DdD_{\mathrm s}-D_{\mathrm d} (Ch. 15: the two differ by a factor of 2.32.3 at zl=0.5,zs=2.0z_l=0.5,\ z_s=2.0, and nothing about that gotcha goes away just because it’s buried inside 𝛂\boldsymbol\alpha now). Every distance factor lives inside this one definition, which is exactly why site/guide_src/lensing.py’s own module docstring can say “the lens-modeling likelihood in this repo is entirely angular — no cosmology enters it” (site/guide_src/lensing.py:9-12): once 𝛂\boldsymbol\alpha is built, it is a pure function of 𝛉\boldsymbol\theta, in arcsec, with every DD already folded away.

With that scaling in hand, the lens equation is a statement about where light appears to come from versus where it actually came from: the apparent, observed position 𝛉\boldsymbol\theta and the true source position 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta differ by exactly the deflection accumulated along the way,

𝛃=𝛉−𝛂(𝛉). \boldsymbol\beta = \boldsymbol\theta - \boldsymbol\alpha(\boldsymbol\theta). \label{eq:lenseq}
