Every symbol in $\eqref{eq:lenseq}$ is an angle. 𝛉\boldsymbol\theta is where you point a telescope; 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta is where the source would be if nothing were in the way; 𝛂(𝛉)\boldsymbol\alpha(\boldsymbol\theta) is what the mass along that line of sight cost you, in arcsec, to get from one to the other.

Differentiate $\eqref{eq:lenseq}$ once and you get the object the rest of Part IV spends three chapters decomposing, the lens Jacobian

A(𝛉)≡∂𝛃∂𝛉=I−∂𝛂∂𝛉. A(\boldsymbol\theta) \;\equiv\; \frac{\partial\boldsymbol\beta}{\partial\boldsymbol\theta} \;=\; I - \frac{\partial\boldsymbol\alpha}{\partial\boldsymbol\theta}. \label{eq:lensjac}

Ch. 6 already leaned on exactly this definition — using 𝛂=∇ψ\boldsymbol\alpha=\nabla\psi and a trace argument — to show A=I−Hψ=(1−κ)I−ΓA=I-H_\psi=(1-\kappa)I-\Gamma; Ch. 5 diagonalizes that split, and Ch. 18 takes its determinant to get magnification. This chapter needs AA for something more basic first: whether $\eqref{eq:lenseq}$ has one solution at all, or more than one.

If 𝛂\boldsymbol\alpha happened to be linear in 𝛉\boldsymbol\theta, the question would have a boring answer. One of this repo’s own deflection fields genuinely is: external shear, L.shear_deflection (site/guide_src/lensing.py:93-95), 𝛂(𝛉)=(γ1θ1+γ2θ2,γ2θ1−γ1θ2)\boldsymbol\alpha(\boldsymbol\theta)=(\gamma_1\theta_1+\gamma_2\theta_2,\ \gamma_2\theta_1-\gamma_1\theta_2), is linear in 𝛉\boldsymbol\theta by construction. For a linear 𝛂\boldsymbol\alpha, AA in $\eqref{eq:lensjac}$ is a constant matrix, $\eqref{eq:lenseq}$ is a linear equation, and (whenever AA is invertible) it has exactly one solution, 𝛉=A−1𝛃\boldsymbol\theta=A^{-1}\boldsymbol\beta, for every 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta. Shear alone never multiplies an image; it only shifts and stretches the one you already have. Every real lens model in this repo pairs shear with an EPL or SIE mass profile precisely because those deflections are not linear — and nonlinearity is the entire reason strong lensing can produce more than one image in the first place.

You already know this

Given 𝛉\boldsymbol\theta, computing 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta from $\eqref{eq:lenseq}$ is one function evaluation — this repo’s own image renderer does exactly this, looping over every pixel 𝛉\boldsymbol\theta in the image plane and evaluating 𝛃(𝛉)\boldsymbol\beta(\boldsymbol\theta) directly (.../gigalens/jax/simulator.py:53-59, cited in full in “Connect to the repo”). Given 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta, finding every 𝛉\boldsymbol\theta that produced it is a different and harder problem: root-finding on a map that need not be one-to-one. That is the same asymmetry as sampling a generative model — running the generator forward is cheap — versus finding every latent that could have produced a given observation, which may have zero, one, or many answers depending on whether the generator happens to be injective there.

For a circularly symmetric mass — the singular isothermal sphere (SIS) of Chapter 16 — 𝛂\boldsymbol\alpha always points radially, with a magnitude that depends only on |𝛉||\boldsymbol\theta|. Put the source on the positive θ1\theta_1-axis at β0≥0\beta_0\ge0; every image then lies on that same axis too, so the full 2-D problem collapses to one real equation in one real unknown θ\theta, where a negative θ\theta is shorthand for “the opposite side of the lens center.” L.sis_deflection (site/guide_src/lensing.py:54-62), evaluated along θ2=0\theta_2=0, is exactly α1(θ)=θEsign(θ)\alpha_1(\theta)=\theta_{\mathrm E}\,\mathrm{sign}(\theta): constant modulus, direction only. $\eqref{eq:lenseq}$ becomes the scalar equation

β0=θ−θEsign(θ). \beta_0 = \theta - \theta_{\mathrm E}\,\mathrm{sign}(\theta).

Plot the right-hand side against θ\theta and read off every θ\theta where the curve crosses the horizontal line β=β0\beta=\beta_0: that is solving the lens equation graphically.

Read the same answer off algebra by splitting on the sign of θ\theta. For θ>0\theta>0: β0=θ−θE\beta_0=\theta-\theta_{\mathrm E}, so θ=β0+θE\theta=\beta_0+\theta_{\mathrm E} — positive whenever β0≥0\beta_0\ge0, so this root always exists. For θ<0\theta<0: β0=θ+θE\beta_0=\theta+\theta_{\mathrm E}, so θ=β0−θE\theta=\beta_0-\theta_{\mathrm E} — negative only if β0<θE\beta_0<\theta_{\mathrm E}. At θE=1″\theta_{\mathrm E}=1'', β0=0.4″\beta_0=0.4'' (Figure 17.1’s own numbers), the two roots are

θ=1.4″andθ=−0.6″ \theta = 1.4'' \quad\text{and}\quad \theta = -0.6''

, two images: a double. worked_examples.py’s ch17_lens_equation checks both against a numerical solver — scipy.optimize.brentq, bracketing each branch of the same L.sis_deflection used above, not a reimplementation — and finds agreement to within 10−810^{-8} on both , essentially floating-point exact. For the SIS, algebra and root-finding agree because algebra is available at all; Ch. 22’s production EPL+shear model has no closed-form inverse, and — per the tip above — gigalens never needs one, because it never solves $\eqref{eq:lenseq}$ for θ\theta in the first place.

One more fact falls out of the same two roots for free. Their separation is

|θ1−θ2|=(β0+θE)−(β0−θE)=2θE |\theta_1-\theta_2| = (\beta_0+\theta_{\mathrm E}) - (\beta_0-\theta_{\mathrm E}) = 2\theta_{\mathrm E}

, and β0\beta_0 cancels completely. For an SIS double, the image separation measures 2θE2\theta_{\mathrm E} directly, regardless of exactly where inside the Einstein radius the source sits. That cancellation is the algebraic fact underneath Chapter 19’s Einstein-radius measurements: an image separation is a distance you can rule with a caliper on a real image, and it converts to θE\theta_{\mathrm E} by nothing harder than dividing by two.

Multiple images

Ask when $\eqref{eq:lenseq}$ can have more than one root for a fixed 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta. In 1-D, the right-hand side g(θ)=θ−α(θ)g(\theta)=\theta-\alpha(\theta) has exactly one root per value of β\beta whenever gg is monotonic — a strictly increasing (or decreasing) function crosses any horizontal line exactly once, by definition of “crosses a line.” Its derivative is g′(θ)=1−α′(θ)g'(\theta)=1-\alpha'(\theta), which by $\eqref{eq:lensjac}$ is nothing but AA itself in one dimension. So gg stops being monotonic exactly where AA changes sign — where α′(θ)\alpha'(\theta) crosses 11. That is not a coincidence offered on faith: A=0A=0 is precisely Chapter 18’s definition of a critical curve, and this section’s whole account of multiple imaging is the 1-D, un-signed-determinant preview of that chapter’s 2-D one. A deflection has to bend “hard enough somewhere” (α′>1\alpha'>1) for gg to fold and produce more than one root; a deflection with α′<1\alpha'<1 everywhere can only ever produce a single image, whatever 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta is.

Apply that to the SIS split above: two roots exist only for |β0|<θE|\beta_0|<\theta_{\mathrm E} — source inside the Einstein radius — and only one for |β0|≥θE|\beta_0|\ge\theta_{\mathrm E}. Push the same source outward, to β0=1.5″\beta_0=1.5'' with θE=1″\theta_{\mathrm E}=1'' still, and the major image survives at θ=β0+θE=2.5″\theta=\beta_0+\theta_{\mathrm E}=2.5'' , but the minor-image branch’s candidate, θ=β0−θE=0.5″\theta=\beta_0-\theta_{\mathrm E}=0.5'' , is not negative — it contradicts the assumption (θ<0\theta<0) it was derived under. There is no second root, full stop; the minor image does not merely fade, it is not a solution. worked_examples.py --show ch17 confirms this the hard way, not just algebraically: asking scipy.optimize.brentq to bracket a sign change on that branch raises ValueError — there genuinely is no root to find , which is a different and stronger statement than “a very faint one.”

Push β0\beta_0 the other way, to exactly 00, and the two 1-D roots collide at ±θE\pm\theta_{\mathrm E} — but the 1-D reduction hides what really happens at exact alignment. With a circularly symmetric lens and the source dead-center behind it, every azimuthal angle around the circle of radius θE\theta_{\mathrm E} is an equally valid image, because the full problem has a continuous rotational symmetry that choosing “the θ1\theta_1-axis” silently threw away. The image is not two points; it is a full circle, the Einstein ring this repository’s own reproductions are named after.

Three words cover almost every strong lens actually observed: a double (two images, the generic case above), a ring (the measure-zero perfectly-aligned case), or a quad (four images). A quad needs more than circular symmetry: Chapter 18’s astroid caustic, produced by an elliptical mass (q<1q<1, SIE or EPL — Ch. 20), is where a source can sit inside a region bounded by two nested folds and pick up two extra roots. A classical result in lensing theory (Burke 1981) sharpens this further: for any smooth, non-singular convergence, the total image count is always odd. The SIS above does not violate that theorem — it is exempt from it, because the SIS is deliberately singular (κSIS=θE/2θ\kappa_{\mathrm{SIS}}=\theta_{\mathrm E}/2\theta diverges as θ→0\theta\to0, Ch. 6). The theorem’s “missing” odd image sits, in principle, exactly at that singularity, arbitrarily demagnified; this repo’s own sie_deflection (site/guide_src/lensing.py:65-78) adds a tiny core radius ss purely to keep that division well-defined in floating point, not because the model asserts a physically resolved core. That is the reason surveys report doubles and quads — even counts — rather than the odd counts a smoother mass distribution would formally guarantee.

The ψ\psi–α\alpha–κ\kappa trio

Three objects, one potential, a loop that started in Ch. 6 and closes here.

The trio, assembled

Object Defining relation Reads as Chapter
ψ(𝛉)\psi(\boldsymbol\theta) sourced by mass via the ln⁡r\ln r Green’s function the lensing potential Ch. 6
𝛂=∇ψ\boldsymbol\alpha=\nabla\psi first derivative of ψ\psi the deflection; bends light Ch. 6, Ch. 16
κ=12∇2ψ\kappa=\tfrac12\nabla^2\psi trace of the second derivative the mass, in Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} units Ch. 6, Ch. 15
𝛃=𝛉−𝛂\boldsymbol\beta=\boldsymbol\theta-\boldsymbol\alpha $\eqref{eq:lenseq}$, this chapter maps an image to its source Ch. 17
A=∂𝛃/∂𝛉=(1−κ)I−ΓA=\partial\boldsymbol\beta/\partial\boldsymbol\theta=(1-\kappa)I-\Gamma $\eqref{eq:lensjac}$, split in Ch. 5 governs multiplicity here, magnification in Ch. 18 Ch. 5, Ch. 17, Ch. 18

Read the table top to bottom and you have this repository’s entire strong-lensing forward model in five lines: mass sources a potential, the potential’s gradient bends light, the lens equation turns that bend into an observed position, and the same potential’s second derivative — split into an isotropic part κ\kappa and a traceless part Γ\Gamma — is exactly the Jacobian whose folding (established this chapter for the SIS) Chapter 18 turns into a signed magnification.

None of this repo’s production code ever materializes ψ\psi itself. The gigalens EPL and SIE profiles hand you closed-form 𝛂\boldsymbol\alpha directly — someone did the Green’s-function convolution by hand, once, for these specific profiles, and the code inherits the answer without ever writing ψ(𝛉)\psi(\boldsymbol\theta) down. What makes that shortcut trustworthy is exactly the curl-free identity Ch. 6 proved: ∇×(∇ψ)≡0\nabla\times(\nabla\psi)\equiv0 for any ψ\psi, so any candidate 𝛂\boldsymbol\alpha that failed the corresponding check (∂αθ1/∂θ2=∂αθ2/∂θ1\partial\alpha_{\theta_1}/\partial\theta_2=\partial\alpha_{\theta_2}/\partial\theta_1) could not have come from a potential at all — and would not be a legitimate deflection to plug into $\eqref{eq:lenseq}$, however smooth it looked on paper. The trio is not three independent facts about lensing; it is one constraint (ψ\psi exists) with three readouts.

Connect to the repo

  • site/guide_src/lensing.py:54-62 (sis_deflection) — the SIS deflection this chapter roots, both algebraically and with scipy.optimize.brentq.
  • site/guide_src/lensing.py:93-95 (shear_deflection) — the one deflection field in this repo that is exactly linear, hence provably incapable of multiplying an image on its own.
  • site/guide_src/lensing.py:101-123 (lens_jacobian) — $\eqref{eq:lensjac}$, computed by central differences on the lens equation itself, exactly as defined here.
  • site/guide_src/figures.py:120-139 (lens_equation_1d) — Figure 17.1’s generator; change beta0 and every number this chapter derives changes with it, because the figure and the algebra above read the same two lines.
  • reproductions/claude-giga-lens/vendor/gigalens-sean/src/gigalens/jax/simulator.py:53-59 (_beta) — the production forward direction of $\eqref{eq:lenseq}$: loop over every image-plane pixel 𝛉\boldsymbol\theta, evaluate 𝛃(𝛉)\boldsymbol\beta(\boldsymbol\theta) directly, sum over every mass component. No root-finding anywhere in sight, because rendering an image never requires inverting the lens equation — only evaluating it.

Exercises

Exercise 17.1 — solve the lens equation by hand

Using Figure 17.1’s own numbers, θE=1″\theta_{\mathrm E}=1'', β0=0.4″\beta_0=0.4'': split the SIS lens equation β0=θ−θEsign(θ)\beta_0=\theta-\theta_{\mathrm E}\,\mathrm{sign}(\theta) on the sign of θ\theta and solve each branch. Confirm both roots against worked_examples.py --show ch17.

Solution

For θ>0\theta>0: 0.4=θ−1⇒θ=1.40.4=\theta-1\Rightarrow\theta=1.4, and 1.4>01.4>0, so this root is valid. For θ<0\theta<0: 0.4=θ+1⇒θ=−0.60.4=\theta+1\Rightarrow\theta=-0.6, and −0.6<0-0.6<0, so this root is valid too. Two roots, a double: θ=1.4″\theta=1.4'' and θ=−0.6″\theta=-0.6'' , matching ch17_lens_equation’s image_1 and image_2 exactly.

Exercise 17.2 — the separation is invariant to where the source sits

Redo Exercise 17.1 with θE=1″\theta_{\mathrm E}=1'' still, but β0=0.9″\beta_0=0.9'' instead of 0.4″0.4''. Find the two new image positions and their separation. What changed, and what didn’t?

Solution

For θ>0\theta>0: θ=0.9+1=1.9\theta=0.9+1=1.9. For θ<0\theta<0: θ=0.9−1=−0.1\theta=0.9-1=-0.1, still negative, so still a valid double. Both image positions moved (from 1.4,−0.61.4,-0.6 to 1.9,−0.11.9,-0.1), but the separation is 1.9−(−0.1)=2.01.9-(-0.1)=2.0 — unchanged. That is not a coincidence of this particular pair of numbers: the derivation in “The lens equation” showed |θ1−θ2|=2θE|\theta_1-\theta_2|=2\theta_{\mathrm E} with β0\beta_0 cancelling algebraically, so the answer must equal the same this chapter already computed at β0=0.4\beta_0=0.4, for any β0\beta_0 inside the Einstein radius. Image separation measures θE\theta_{\mathrm E}; it does not measure where the source is.

Exercise 17.3 — when does the minor image disappear?

Still with θE=1″\theta_{\mathrm E}=1'': at what value of β0\beta_0 does the SIS stop producing two images? For β0=1.5″\beta_0=1.5'', find the surviving image’s position, and show algebraically why the second branch has no valid solution (don’t just say “it’s very faint”).

Solution

From the split in “Multiple images”, the θ<0\theta<0 branch requires β0<θE=1\beta_0<\theta_{\mathrm E}=1; at β0=1.5\beta_0=1.5 that condition fails, so the transition happens at β0=θE=1″\beta_0=\theta_{\mathrm E}=1'' exactly. The surviving (major) image is at θ=β0+θE=2.5″\theta=\beta_0+\theta_{\mathrm E}=2.5'' . The candidate for the other branch is θ=β0−θE=0.5″\theta=\beta_0-\theta_{\mathrm E}=0.5'' , which is not negative — it violates the θ<0\theta<0 assumption used to derive it, so it is not a solution of the original equation at all, not a demagnified one. worked_examples.py’s ch17_lens_equation confirms this by trying to bracket a root there with scipy.optimize.brentq and getting a ValueError (no sign change) instead of a tiny number .

Exercise 17.4 — close the trio: from ψ\psi to images, in one pass

Ch. 6, Exercise 6.3 gave the SIS potential ψSIS(θ)=θEθ\psi_{\mathrm{SIS}}(\theta)=\theta_{\mathrm E}\,\theta and found ∇ψSIS=θEθ̂\nabla\psi_{\mathrm{SIS}}=\theta_{\mathrm E}\,\hat\theta (constant modulus θE\theta_{\mathrm E}, radially outward). Starting only from that gradient — not from L.sis_deflection — rebuild the SIS lens equation along the θ1\theta_1-axis and re-derive this chapter’s two image positions at θE=1″\theta_{\mathrm E}=1'', β0=0.4″\beta_0=0.4''.

Solution

Restricted to the θ1\theta_1-axis, “radially outward at constant modulus θE\theta_{\mathrm E}” means α1(θ)=θE\alpha_1(\theta)=\theta_{\mathrm E} for θ>0\theta>0 and α1(θ)=−θE\alpha_1(\theta)=-\theta_{\mathrm E} for θ<0\theta<0 — i.e. α1(θ)=θEsign(θ)\alpha_1(\theta)=\theta_{\mathrm E}\,\mathrm{sign}(\theta), exactly the deflection this chapter used, now obtained purely from $\eqref{eq:lensjac}$’s partner identity 𝛂=∇ψ\boldsymbol\alpha=\nabla\psi rather than from L.sis_deflection directly. Substituting into $\eqref{eq:lenseq}$ reproduces the same scalar equation, β0=θ−θEsign(θ)\beta_0=\theta-\theta_{\mathrm E}\,\mathrm{sign}(\theta), whose roots were already found in Exercise 17.1: θ=1.4″\theta=1.4'' and θ=−0.6″\theta=-0.6'' . The trio table’s top row and bottom row meet: a potential written down in one line in Chapter 6 predicts, by nothing but differentiation and this chapter’s algebra, exactly where the two images of a real source would land.

18. Magnification, critical curves, and caustics

Chapter 17 gave you the lens equation, 𝛃=𝛉−𝛂(𝛉)\boldsymbol\beta = \boldsymbol\theta - \boldsymbol\alpha(\boldsymbol\theta) (Ch. 17), and the fact that it can have more than one solution for a single source. This chapter answers the two questions that follow immediately: how bright is each of those solutions, and where, exactly, does a second one come from? Both answers are the same object, differentiated once — the lens Jacobian A≡∂𝛃/∂𝛉A \equiv \partial\boldsymbol\beta/\partial\boldsymbol\theta, whose determinant Chapter 4 already told you is a literal area ratio. Its reciprocal is the magnification. The curve where it vanishes is a critical curve. The image of that curve under the lens map is a caustic. And crossing a caustic is the precise mechanism by which a second, third, or fourth image is born. By the end of this chapter you can compute all four — magnification, critical curve, caustic, and the parity of an image — from nothing but a deflection field and the differentiation Chapter 4 already taught you, and check every one of them against a number this repository’s own figure-generation code and production forward model actually compute.

What you can skip

Chapter 4 already derived that |det⁡J||\det J| is a local area-scaling factor and opened the Log-Det Ledger with μ=1/|det⁡A|\mu = 1/|\det A| as row 1 — if that chapter is fresh, skip straight to Magnification is a Jacobian for the lensing-specific radial/tangential split, or to Critical curves if you also recall that a symmetric matrix’s determinant is the product of its eigenvalues (Chapter 5). What is not boilerplate: why the sign of det⁡A\det A, not just its magnitude, carries distinct physical information (Parity), and why a curve that shrinks to a single point in the image plane does not shrink to a point in the source plane (Caustics) — a fact this repository’s own figure code spends a paragraph justifying because it is genuinely unintuitive the first time.

Magnification is a Jacobian

The lens Jacobian is the derivative of the lens equation, taken exactly the way Chapter 4 defines a Jacobian:

A≡∂𝛃∂𝛉=I−∂𝛂∂𝛉. A \;\equiv\; \frac{\partial \boldsymbol\beta}{\partial \boldsymbol\theta} \;=\; I - \frac{\partial \boldsymbol\alpha}{\partial \boldsymbol\theta}. \label{eq:jacA}

Because 𝛂=∇ψ\boldsymbol\alpha = \nabla\psi for a scalar lensing potential ψ\psi (Ch. 6), ∂𝛂/∂𝛉\partial\boldsymbol\alpha/\partial\boldsymbol\theta is a Hessian, and Chapter 4 already proved a gradient field’s Jacobian is automatically symmetric (Ch. 4). So AA is symmetric at every image position, before any lens-specific physics is chosen — which is exactly what lets Chapter 5’s general fact about symmetric 2×22\times2 matrices apply here: AA diagonalizes in a real, orthonormal eigenbasis (Ch. 5).

A short physical argument fixes what 1/det⁡A1/\det A means. Light travel conserves photon number — no absorption, no emission along a vacuum ray path — so surface brightness (flux per unit solid angle) is the same at the source and at the image. A tiny image-plane patch of solid angle dΩθd\Omega_\theta maps, under $\eqref{eq:jacA}$’s local linearization, to a source-plane patch of solid angle dΩβ=|det⁡A|dΩθd\Omega_\beta = |\det A|\,d\Omega_\theta (Chapter 4’s area-ratio argument, applied to AA specifically). Flip that around: the image occupies a solid angle dΩβ/|det⁡A|d\Omega_\beta/|\det A| for a fixed intrinsic source patch, so a bigger apparent patch at the same surface brightness means more total flux, by a factor 1/|det⁡A|1/|\det A|. That factor is the magnification, and its signed version is what this repository — and this guide — call μ\mu:

μ≡1det⁡A. \mu \;\equiv\; \frac{1}{\det A}. \label{eq:mu}

site/guide_src/lensing.py:139 (magnification) computes exactly $\eqref{eq:mu}$, and its own docstring states this chapter’s opening claim in one line: “This is the SAME change-of-variables factor that a normalizing flow applies as −log⁡|det⁡J|-\log|\det J|.” Chapter 4 opened the Log-Det Ledger with this fact stated abstractly, before this book had a lens equation to check it against. Here is the check.

For a circularly symmetric deflection field, 𝛂(𝛉)=α(r)𝛉̂\boldsymbol\alpha(\boldsymbol\theta) = \alpha(r)\,\hat{\boldsymbol\theta} with r=|𝛉|r = |\boldsymbol\theta|, symmetry does the eigendecomposition for you: at any point, the eigenvectors of AA are simply the local radial and tangential directions. Move a small step dθrd\theta_r purely radially, and the deflection changes by α′(r)dθr\alpha'(r)\,d\theta_r in the same radial direction — giving a radial eigenvalue Arr=1−α′(r)A_{rr} = 1 - \alpha'(r). Move a small step dθtd\theta_t purely tangentially instead: this rotates your position by an angle dθt/rd\theta_t/r, and by circular symmetry the deflection vector rotates by that identical angle, which displaces it tangentially by α(r)⋅(dθt/r)\alpha(r)\cdot(d\theta_t/r) — giving a tangential eigenvalue Att=1−α(r)/rA_{tt} = 1 - \alpha(r)/r. So

det⁡A=ArrAtt=(1−α′(r))(1−α(r)r). \det A = A_{rr}A_{tt} = \bigl(1-\alpha'(r)\bigr)\left(1-\frac{\alpha(r)}{r}\right).

Apply this to the singular isothermal sphere, α(r)=θE\alpha(r) = \theta_{\mathrm{E}} (lensing.py:54, sis_deflection) — a constant-modulus deflection, “the flat rotation curve of a galaxy in one line: the deflection does not care how far out you are, only which way” (lensing.py:57-58). Constant α\alpha means α′(r)=0\alpha'(r) = 0 identically, so Arr=1A_{rr} = 1 for every r>0r > 0: an SIS has no radial critical curve at all, ever — only Att=1−θE/rA_{tt} = 1 - \theta_{\mathrm{E}}/r can vanish. That gives a magnification

μ(r)=11−θE/r=rr−θE. \mu(r) = \frac{1}{1-\theta_{\mathrm{E}}/r} = \frac{r}{r-\theta_{\mathrm{E}}}.

At θE=1″\theta_{\mathrm{E}} = 1'' and an image at r=2″r = 2'', this predicts μ=2\mu = 2 . lensing.py:101 (lens_jacobian) never sees this formula — it differentiates sis_deflection numerically, by central differences, and magnification takes 1/det⁡A1/\det A of the result. That purely numerical route gives μ=1.999999999962\mu = 1.999999999962 , agreeing with the closed form to 3.8×10−113.8\times10^{-11} — a Jacobian built from finite differences, matching an analytic eigenvalue argument to ten decimal places. worked_examples.py --show ch18 reproduces both numbers directly.

Log-Det Ledger — row 1, paid off

Chapter 4 opened this ledger with μ=1/|det⁡A|\mu = 1/|\det A| stated abstractly. This section supplies everything that was missing: AA is the derivative of a real lens equation (Ch. 17), μ=1/det⁡A\mu = 1/\det A is computed by a genuine Jacobian differentiation (lensing.py:101-146), and the result is checked against a closed-form eigenvalue argument to machine precision. Row 1 is not a metaphor for the rest of this book — it is arithmetic that reproduces.

Critical curves

A critical curve is the locus {𝛉:det⁡A(𝛉)=0}\{\boldsymbol\theta : \det A(\boldsymbol\theta) = 0\}. There, μ\mu formally diverges: a point source placed exactly on the corresponding caustic (below) would be infinitely magnified. Real sources have finite extent and real telescopes have a PSF (Ch. 11), so nothing in an actual image is literally infinite — but images that straddle a critical curve get very bright and very stretched, which is exactly what a giant arc is.

Because det⁡A=ArrAtt\det A = A_{rr}A_{tt}, it vanishes when either eigenvalue vanishes on its own, and those are two geometrically distinct curves: a tangential critical curve (Att=0A_{tt}=0) and a radial critical curve (Arr=0A_{rr}=0). The SIS above has only the first — Arr≡1A_{rr} \equiv 1 never crosses zero. A singular isothermal ellipsoid (SIE, q<1q < 1) has both, because breaking circular symmetry lets the deflection field’s radial derivative do something an SIS’s never can.

You already know this

A critical curve is where the lensing Jacobian becomes singular — exactly the condition a normalizing flow’s bijector is engineered to forbid everywhere (a well-built flow keeps det⁡J\det J bounded away from zero, precisely so log⁡|det⁡J|\log|\det J| never blows up). The lens equation carries no such constraint: nothing stops det⁡A\det A from crossing zero, and when it does, the map stops being locally invertible in one direction — which is the entire mechanism behind multiple imaging. A flow is built to never do what a lens does routinely.

The radial critical curve’s disappearing act is a direct consequence of the profile being singular: convergence κ∼1/R\kappa \sim 1/R diverges as R→0R\to0 (Ch. 20), and as the regularizing core radius lensing.py:65 (sie_deflection’s s argument) shrinks toward zero, the small oval where Arr=0A_{rr}=0 shrinks with it, collapsing onto the single point 𝛉=𝟎\boldsymbol\theta = \boldsymbol 0 in the exactly singular limit. You might expect its caustic to collapse to a point too. It does not — which is the subject of the next section.

Caustics

A caustic is the image of a critical curve under the lens map: push every point on {det⁡A=0}\{\det A = 0\} through 𝛃=𝛉−𝛂(𝛉)\boldsymbol\beta = \boldsymbol\theta - \boldsymbol\alpha(\boldsymbol\theta) and plot where it lands in the source plane. The word is borrowed from ordinary optics — the same bright, curved lines that form at the bottom of a swimming pool, or on the wall behind a wine glass, are caustics of a completely different (but equally singular) map. Figure 18.1’s right panel is one: the tangential branch’s caustic is the astroid, a four-cusped closed curve, small compared to θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}}.

Here is why crossing a smooth stretch of caustic — away from a cusp — always changes the image count by exactly two, never one or three. Near such a point, exactly one eigenvalue of AA vanishes; call its eigendirection ∥\parallel and the other ⟂\perp. Because A∥∥A_{\parallel\parallel} is a smooth function of position that happens to equal zero right there, the first surviving term in a Taylor expansion of β∥\beta_\parallel along the ∥\parallel direction is quadratic, not linear — precisely Chapter 2’s argument for why a stationary point needs a second-order term to resolve it at all (Ch. 2):

β∥(θ∥)≈β∥,0+cθ∥2,c≠0. \beta_\parallel(\theta_\parallel) \;\approx\; \beta_{\parallel,0} + c\,\theta_\parallel^2, \qquad c \ne 0.

Solving for θ∥\theta_\parallel given a source position β∥\beta_\parallel gives θ∥=±(β∥−β∥,0)/c\theta_\parallel = \pm\sqrt{(\beta_\parallel-\beta_{\parallel,0})/c}: two real solutions on one side of β∥,0\beta_{\parallel,0}, none on the other. A source crossing the caustic point β∥,0\beta_{\parallel,0} therefore gains or loses exactly one pair of images, born or annihilated together right at the critical curve (where μ\mu diverges, consistent with the two roots merging as β∥→β∥,0\beta_\parallel\to\beta_{\parallel,0}). This is the fold catastrophe — the same local algebra as a saddle-node bifurcation in a dynamical system, a stable and unstable fixed point annihilating each other as a parameter crosses a threshold. The astroid’s four cusps are points where two folds meet, and crossing through one adds a further pair; a source deep inside the astroid sees more images than one just inside a smooth edge.

The radial branch’s caustic is the more surprising object, and this repository’s own comment explains why in one line: as the regularizing core shrinks, the radial critical curve shrinks to the single point 𝛉=𝟎\boldsymbol\theta=\boldsymbol0, but its deflection there does not vanish — 𝛂(𝟎)\boldsymbol\alpha(\boldsymbol0) stays finite, of order θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}}, exactly the same “flat rotation curve” fact used above, and its direction still depends on which way you approached the origin. So walk a vanishingly small circle of radius ε\varepsilon around the center, parametrized by angle ϕ\phi so that 𝛉=ε(cos⁡ϕ,sin⁡ϕ)\boldsymbol\theta = \varepsilon(\cos\phi,\sin\phi), and push it through the lens equation: 𝛃(ε,ϕ)=ε(cos⁡ϕ,sin⁡ϕ)−𝛂(ε,ϕ)→−𝛂(0,ϕ)\boldsymbol\beta(\varepsilon,\phi) = \varepsilon(\cos\phi,\sin\phi) - \boldsymbol\alpha(\varepsilon,\phi) \to -\boldsymbol\alpha(0,\phi) as ε→0\varepsilon\to0 — an O(θE)O(\theta_{\mathrm{E}})-sized closed curve, not a point, because the limit keeps all of 𝛂\boldsymbol\alpha’s angular structure even as the circle it came from shrinks away. This is site/guide_src/figures.py:176-195’s construction exactly, and it is why a curve that vanishes in the image plane still produces a full curve — this chapter’s cut — in the source plane. site/guide_src/worked_examples.py’s ch18_magnification reproduces the same number (0.8102368876963119) by an independent bisection/angular-sampling route rather than importing the figure code, and the two agree to machine precision .

The repository’s own docstring states the cut’s role in image counting directly: “inside the cut a source has two images; outside it has one” (site/guide_src/figures.py:156-157) — a second, genuine (if tiny, at this core radius) fold, nested inside the astroid’s. A circular lens has no such second fold: its only critical curve is the full Einstein ring, and the entire ring degenerates to the single caustic point 𝛃=0\boldsymbol\beta=0, leaving nothing to nest a further transition inside. Solving the SIS lens equation directly (as this chapter already has) shows its own image count still changes, from one to two — but at |𝛃|=θE|\boldsymbol\beta|=\theta_{\mathrm{E}}, not at the caustic point itself: the second image does not meet a partner at a smooth critical curve there, it shrinks straight into the profile’s singular center (r2=θE−β→0r_2 = \theta_{\mathrm{E}}-\beta \to 0) and disappears — a different, singularity-driven way for an image to vanish, not a fold. An SIE’s genuine second critical curve is why real strong lenses come as doubles and quads — the observational names for exactly the multiplicity regions Figure 18.1’s right panel draws.

Parity

μ=1/det⁡A\mu = 1/\det A is signed, not just an area ratio. lensing.py:140 says it plainly: “Signed: negative μ\mu means a parity-flipped image.” Chapter 4’s Exercise 4.4 asked what a negative det⁡A\det A could mean physically, before this book had a lens equation to answer with. Now it does.

det⁡A=ArrAtt\det A = A_{rr}A_{tt} changes sign exactly when one eigenvalue changes sign while the other does not — which is exactly what happens at a critical curve. In the fold analysis above, the two newly created images have local slopes dβ∥/dθ∥=2cθ∥d\beta_\parallel/d\theta_\parallel = 2c\,\theta_\parallel of opposite sign (one at +θ∥+\theta_\parallel, one at −θ∥-\theta_\parallel): one image preserves orientation, the other reverses it. A positive-parity (μ>0\mu>0) image looks like the source, rotated and stretched; a negative-parity (μ<0\mu<0) image is its mirror image, not just its magnified copy.

The SIS worked example already contains both signs. At r=2″r=2'' (outside θE=1″\theta_{\mathrm{E}}=1'', only one image exists there), μ=+2\mu=+2: direct parity, magnified. At r=0.5″r=0.5'' — inside θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}}, where Att=1−θE/r=1−2=−1A_{tt} = 1-\theta_{\mathrm{E}}/r = 1-2 = -1 while ArrA_{rr} stays +1+1 — the same numerical Jacobian gives μ=−1\mu = -1 , matching the closed form r/(r−θE)=0.5/(−0.5)r/(r-\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) = 0.5/(-0.5) to 4.0×10−104.0\times10^{-10} . This is the SIS’s second image — the one an Einstein-cross or a double-lens configuration always has a counterpart of — and |μ|=1|\mu|=1 there: it carries exactly the source’s own flux, neither magnified nor demagnified, only flipped. Magnitude and sign are independent axes of the same number; a magnification of exactly 11 is not “no lensing,” it can be a full mirror flip.

Exercises

Exercise 18.1 — the radial/tangential split, from scratch

For a circularly symmetric deflection field α(r)\alpha(r), this chapter asserted Arr=1−α′(r)A_{rr} = 1-\alpha'(r) and Att=1−α(r)/rA_{tt} = 1-\alpha(r)/r from a symmetry argument. Confirm it by direct differentiation: write α1(θ1,θ2)=α(ρ)θ1/ρ\alpha_1(\theta_1,\theta_2) = \alpha(\rho)\,\theta_1/\rho and α2(θ1,θ2)=α(ρ)θ2/ρ\alpha_2(\theta_1,\theta_2) = \alpha(\rho)\,\theta_2/\rho with ρ=θ12+θ22\rho=\sqrt{\theta_1^2+\theta_2^2}, and compute ∂α1/∂θ1\partial\alpha_1/\partial\theta_1 and ∂α2/∂θ2\partial\alpha_2/\partial\theta_2 at the point (θ1,θ2)=(r,0)(\theta_1,\theta_2)=(r,0).

Solution

∂α1/∂θ1=α′(ρ)(θ1ρ)2+α(ρ)θ22ρ3\partial\alpha_1/\partial\theta_1 = \alpha'(\rho)\left(\frac{\theta_1}{\rho}\right)^2 + \alpha(\rho)\,\frac{\theta_2^2}{\rho^3}. At (r,0)(r,0): θ2=0\theta_2=0, θ1/ρ=1\theta_1/\rho=1, so this is α′(r)\alpha'(r), giving a11=1−α′(r)=Arra_{11}=1-\alpha'(r)=A_{rr}.

∂α2/∂θ2=α′(ρ)(θ2ρ)2+α(ρ)θ12ρ3\partial\alpha_2/\partial\theta_2 = \alpha'(\rho)\left(\frac{\theta_2}{\rho}\right)^2 + \alpha(\rho)\,\frac{\theta_1^2}{\rho^3}. At (r,0)(r,0): θ2/ρ=0\theta_2/\rho=0, θ12/ρ3=1/r\theta_1^2/\rho^3=1/r, so this is α(r)/r\alpha(r)/r, giving a22=1−α(r)/r=Atta_{22}=1-\alpha(r)/r=A_{tt}.

Both off-diagonal terms, ∂α1/∂θ2\partial\alpha_1/\partial\theta_2 and ∂α2/∂θ1\partial\alpha_2/\partial\theta_1, carry a factor of θ2\theta_2 that vanishes at (r,0)(r,0) — confirming that the radial/tangential axes really are the eigenbasis there, not just a convenient guess.

Exercise 18.2 — a parity flip you can predict without a computer

Using only μ(r)=r/(r−θE)\mu(r) = r/(r-\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) for the SIS, at what radius does μ=−1\mu = -1 exactly, for θE=1″\theta_{\mathrm{E}}=1''? What does |μ|=1|\mu|=1 combined with a negative sign mean for the resulting image, physically?

Solution

Solve r/(r−1)=−1⇒r=−(r−1)⇒2r=1⇒r=0.5″r/(r-1) = -1 \Rightarrow r = -(r-1) \Rightarrow 2r = 1 \Rightarrow r = 0.5'' — exactly the point this chapter checked numerically . Physically: the image carries precisely the source’s own flux (no brightening, no dimming — |μ|=1|\mu|=1), but it is a mirror image, not a magnified copy, because det⁡A<0\det A<0 there. This resolves Chapter 4’s Exercise 4.4: a sign flip in det⁡A\det A is not a numerical curiosity, it is the difference between “the same shape, bigger” and “the same shape, flipped.”

Exercise 18.3 — why the SIS never shows a quad

Using this chapter’s eigenvalue argument, explain in one or two sentences why a circularly symmetric lens (SIS or SIE with q=1q=1) can never produce four images of a single source, no matter where the source sits, while an SIE with q<1q<1 routinely does.

Solution

A circular lens has Arr≡1A_{rr}\equiv1 for all r>0r>0 (this chapter’s derivation: α(r)=θE\alpha(r)=\theta_{\mathrm{E}} is constant, so α′(r)=0\alpha'(r)=0 identically) — there is no radial critical curve at any nonzero radius, hence nothing to nest a second multiplicity transition inside the tangential one. Its own image count still changes, from one to two, but (as the Caustics section works out) that boundary sits at |𝛃|=θE|\boldsymbol\beta|=\theta_{\mathrm{E}}, where the would-be second image shrinks into the singular center and disappears, rather than meeting a partner at a smooth critical curve — not a fold. An SIE with q<1q<1 breaks the symmetry that forces Arr≡1A_{rr}\equiv1, so it acquires a second, genuine critical curve of its own — and with it, a real fold, a real second multiplicity transition, and the possibility of four images.

Exercise 18.4 — reading Figure 18.1’s numbers as a consistency check

Figure 18.1 reports the tangential critical curve’s extent as 0.9999″0.9999'' along its long axis and 0.6999″0.6999'' along its short axis, for θE=1″\theta_{\mathrm{E}}=1'', q=0.7q=0.7. State the conjecture these numbers support about the exact (s→0s\to0) singular limit, and say what would falsify it.

Solution

The conjecture: in the exactly singular limit, the tangential critical curve touches the principal axes at exactly θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}} and qθEq\,\theta_{\mathrm{E}} — here 1.0″1.0'' and 0.7″0.7'' — with the 0.9999″0.9999''/0.6999″0.6999'' reported values differing from those only because lensing.py:65’s sie_deflection uses a small but nonzero core, s=10−4s=10^{-4}, to regularize the central singularity. It would be falsified by re-running ch18_magnification’s bisection with a smaller s and finding the extents move away from 1.01.0 and 0.70.7 rather than toward them — which is not what happens: shrinking ss from 10−410^{-4} to 10−1010^{-10} moves both numbers past nine nines of agreement with θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}} and qθEq\,\theta_{\mathrm{E}} exactly, the signature of a genuine s→0s\to0 limit rather than a coincidence at one particular core size.

19. The Einstein radius: the one thing lensing measures cleanly

Every number this book eventually argues about — the EPL slope γ\gamma, the external shear, the source’s shape — is a fit: a quantity pulled out of noisy pixels by trusting a model of how the light got there. This chapter is about the one number that is not. The Einstein radius θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}} falls out of pure geometry — where the images are, and how far the lens and source sit from us and each other — and it does so before you commit to any assumption about how mass is arranged inside the lens galaxy. That is why it is the number every lensing paper leads with, the number a photometric pipeline can estimate from a spectrum alone, and the number this repository’s own reproductions reconstruct to a percent or two even from an independent code path. By the end of this chapter you can derive θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}} from a galaxy’s velocity dispersion, explain in one line why the enclosed mass M(<θE)M(<\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) does not care what density profile you assumed, and see both claims checked against this repository’s own numbers. Chapters 20 through 26 spend the rest of the book on γ\gamma, which is a much harder measurement precisely because it does not have this chapter’s kind of protection.

What you can skip

If you already know that an Einstein ring is what a circularly symmetric lens makes of a perfectly aligned source, skip What θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}} is and start at The mean-convergence identity. If you are comfortable setting up and evaluating a definite integral, you can take the projection integral in θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}} from σv\sigma_v on faith and skip straight to the boxed result.

What θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}} is

Recall the lens equation from Ch. 17: 𝛃=𝛉−𝛂(𝛉)\boldsymbol\beta = \boldsymbol\theta - \boldsymbol\alpha(\boldsymbol\theta), mapping an image-plane position 𝛉\boldsymbol\theta to the source-plane position 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta it came from. Now specialize to the cleanest possible geometry: a lens whose mass distribution is circularly symmetric (a good approximation for a single massive elliptical viewed close to face-on), with the source sitting exactly on the optical axis, 𝛃=𝟎\boldsymbol\beta = \mathbf{0}.

Because the lens is circularly symmetric, 𝛂(𝛉)\boldsymbol\alpha(\boldsymbol\theta) points radially and its magnitude depends only on θ=|𝛉|\theta = |\boldsymbol\theta|. Restrict the lens equation to any fixed position angle and it becomes a single scalar equation in the radius alone, θ−α(θ)=0\theta - \alpha(\theta) = 0. Nothing in that equation refers to which direction you picked — so if θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}} solves it, it solves it at every position angle simultaneously. The solution set is not a point; it is an entire circle. That circle is the Einstein ring, and its radius is the Einstein radius θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}}.

Break the alignment even slightly and the ring splits into the discrete images Ch. 17 already introduced — two for a source outside the lens’s inner caustic, four for a source inside it — with typical image separations and arc lengths set by θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}} itself. θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}} is the master angular scale of a lensing system: everything else in the image — the separation of a double, the diameter of a quad, the length of an arc — is a number of order θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}}, not an independent scale.

The mean-convergence identity

The defining condition θE−α(θE)=0\theta_{\mathrm{E}} - \alpha(\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) = 0 looks like it depends on the full shape of α(θ)\alpha(\theta), which in turn depends on the full radial mass profile. It does not. What it depends on is a single number: the average convergence enclosed within θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}}, regardless of how that convergence is arranged inside.

Start from Ch. 6’s statement of the lens equation trio, ∇2ψ=2κ\nabla^2\psi = 2\kappa, 𝛂=∇ψ\boldsymbol\alpha = \nabla\psi. For a circularly symmetric ψ(θ)\psi(\theta), the 2-D Laplacian in polar coordinates acting on a radius-only function is ∇2ψ=θ−1d(θdψ/dθ)/dθ\nabla^2\psi = \theta^{-1}\, d(\theta\, d\psi/d\theta)/d\theta, and the radial deflection is α(θ)=dψ/dθ\alpha(\theta) = d\psi/d\theta. So

1θddθ(θα(θ))=2κ(θ)⇒ddθ(θα(θ))=2θκ(θ). \frac{1}{\theta}\frac{d}{d\theta}\big(\theta\,\alpha(\theta)\big) = 2\kappa(\theta) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{d}{d\theta}\big(\theta\,\alpha(\theta)\big) = 2\,\theta\,\kappa(\theta).

Integrate from 00 to θ\theta — θα(θ)\theta\alpha(\theta) starts at 00 for any profile without a point mass at the center —

θα(θ)=2∫0θκ(t)tdt⇒α(θ)=θκ‾(θ),κ‾(θ)≡2θ2∫0θκ(t)tdt. \theta\,\alpha(\theta) = 2\int_0^\theta \kappa(t)\, t\, dt \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \alpha(\theta) = \theta\,\bar\kappa(\theta), \qquad \bar\kappa(\theta) \equiv \frac{2}{\theta^2}\int_0^\theta \kappa(t)\,t\,dt. \label{eq:alpha-kbar}

κ‾(θ)\bar\kappa(\theta) is the mean convergence enclosed within radius θ\theta — exactly the quantity mean_kappa_within computes at site/guide_src/lensing.py:179. Equation $\eqref{eq:alpha-kbar}$ says the deflection at any radius is fixed entirely by how much convergence sits inside that radius; nothing outside it contributes. (This is the lensing analogue of Newton’s shell theorem: a spherical shell of mass exerts no net force on anything inside it, so only the enclosed mass matters. Same statement, one dimension flatter.)

Now substitute θ=θE\theta = \theta_{\mathrm{E}} into the Einstein-ring condition θE=α(θE)\theta_{\mathrm{E}} = \alpha(\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) from the previous section, and use $\eqref{eq:alpha-kbar}$:

θE=θEκ‾(θE)⇒κ‾(θE)=1. \theta_{\mathrm{E}} = \theta_{\mathrm{E}}\,\bar\kappa(\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bar\kappa(\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) = 1.

This is the whole content of the phrase “Einstein radius”: the radius at which the mean interior convergence is exactly critical. It is a definition, derived from nothing but the Poisson equation and the ring condition — it says nothing about whether the lens is a point mass, an SIS, an SIE, or an EPL with some particular γ\gamma. Any circularly symmetric profile has some radius where its own enclosed mean reaches 1, and that radius is, by construction, what everyone calls θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}}.

Check it numerically on the simplest case, the singular isothermal sphere (SIS), whose convergence is κ(θ)=θE/(2θ)\kappa(\theta) = \theta_{\mathrm{E}}/(2\theta) (derived from first principles in the next section). Evaluating κ‾\bar\kappa by direct quadrature at θ=θE=1\theta = \theta_{\mathrm{E}} = 1 gives 0.9999950.999995 — not exactly 11 only because the numerical integral starts a hair off the origin rather than because the identity is approximate.

θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}} from σv\sigma_v

Ch. 10 derived the isothermal sphere’s 3-D density from hydrostatic equilibrium: ρ(r)=σv2/(2πGr2)\rho(r) = \sigma_v^2/(2\pi G r^2), where σv\sigma_v is the galaxy’s stellar velocity dispersion — a number a spectrum measures directly, with no imaging required. Project that to a surface density with the line-of-sight integral Ch. 3 introduced in general:

Σ(R)=∫−∞∞ρ(R2+z2)dz=σv22πG∫−∞∞dzR2+z2=σv22πG⋅πR=σv22GR. \Sigma(R) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \rho\!\left(\sqrt{R^2+z^2}\right) dz = \frac{\sigma_v^2}{2\pi G}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{dz}{R^2+z^2} = \frac{\sigma_v^2}{2\pi G}\cdot\frac{\pi}{R} = \frac{\sigma_v^2}{2GR}.

The middle integral is [θ↦arctan(z/R)/R]−∞∞=π/R\left[\theta \mapsto \arctan(z/R)/R\right]_{-\infty}^{\infty} = \pi/R — a table integral, no new machinery. This is exactly the ρ∼r−γ⇒Σ∼R1−γ\rho \sim r^{-\gamma} \Rightarrow \Sigma \sim R^{1-\gamma} scaling of Ch. 3 at γ=2\gamma = 2, with the constant filled in.

Convert to convergence with Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} (Ch. 15) and physical radius R=DdθR = D_{\mathrm{d}}\theta: κ(θ)=σv2/(2GDdθΣcr)\kappa(\theta) = \sigma_v^2 / (2GD_{\mathrm{d}}\theta\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}), which has the form A/θA/\theta. Plugging κ(t)=A/t\kappa(t)=A/t into $\eqref{eq:alpha-kbar}$ gives κ‾(θ)=2A/θ\bar\kappa(\theta) = 2A/\theta for any θ\theta — for this particular profile the mean is exactly twice the local value everywhere, not just at θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}}. Setting κ‾(θE)=1\bar\kappa(\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) = 1 gives θE=2A=σv2/(GDdΣcr)\theta_{\mathrm{E}} = 2A = \sigma_v^2/(GD_{\mathrm{d}}\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}). Substitute Σcr=c2Ds/(4πGDdDds)\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} = c^2D_{\mathrm{s}}/(4\pi GD_{\mathrm{d}}D_{\mathrm{ds}}) (Ch. 15) and DdD_{\mathrm{d}} cancels outright:

θE=4π(σvc)2DdsDs. \theta_{\mathrm{E}} = 4\pi\left(\frac{\sigma_v}{c}\right)^2\frac{D_{\mathrm{ds}}}{D_{\mathrm{s}}}. \label{eq:thetaE-sv}

This is Hsu+2025’s Eq. 1, used verbatim at reproductions/hsu-2025/07_classify_einstein_dimple.py:116 and site/guide_src/lensing.py:170. It is quadratic in σv\sigma_v and linear in the distance ratio — and Dds≠Ds−DdD_{\mathrm{ds}} \neq D_{\mathrm{s}} - D_{\mathrm{d}} (Ch. 15) matters here exactly as much as it did there, since DdsD_{\mathrm{ds}} enters $\eqref{eq:thetaE-sv}$ directly.

For a fiducial massive elliptical — σv=250\sigma_v = 250 km/s at zl=0.5z_l=0.5, zs=2.0z_s=2.0, the same system Ch. 10 already quoted — $\eqref{eq:thetaE-sv}$ gives θE=1.145″\theta_{\mathrm{E}} = 1.145'' .

Now apply it to real data. reproductions/cikota-2023 reproduces Cikota et al. 2023’s Einstein cross DESI-253.2534+26.8843 — “a massive elliptical lens galaxy (L1)” (reproductions/cikota-2023/papers/main.tex:69) — on public DESI Legacy imaging, fitting an imaging Einstein radius of 2.103″2.103'' against the paper’s own, higher-resolution 2.520″2.520'' (reproductions/cikota-2023/papers/main.tex:213), and inverting $\eqref{eq:thetaE-sv}$ to read off an implied σSIE=347\sigma_{\mathrm{SIE}} = 347 km/s against the paper’s spectroscopic 379±2379 \pm 2 km/s (reproductions/cikota-2023/papers/main.tex:214). Feed that recovered 347347 km/s back into $\eqref{eq:thetaE-sv}$ at an illustrative lens/source redshift pair — zl=0.271z_l = 0.271, zs=0.897z_s = 0.897, chosen only to exercise the formula at some concrete geometry, not this system’s own spectroscopic redshifts (those are zL1=0.636z_{\mathrm{L1}} = 0.636, zs=2.597z_s = 2.597; see Exercise 19.3 for what using them instead does) — and it returns

θE=2.233″ \theta_{\mathrm{E}} = 2.233''

,

landing between the repository’s own imaging fit (2.103″2.103'') and the published, sharper-PSF fit (2.520″2.520''). That is not a coincidence of the particular redshift pair chosen — 347347 km/s was itself backed out of a θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}} in roughly that range — but it is a genuine sanity check that $\eqref{eq:thetaE-sv}$ is behaving the way a quadratic-in-σv\sigma_v, linear-in-geometry relation should: neither wildly off nor suspiciously exact.

Why does the campaign fit the full image rather than stopping at $\eqref{eq:thetaE-sv}$? Because σv\sigma_v alone is a single scalar — it fixes θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}} but says nothing about ellipticity, position angle, external shear, or the density slope γ\gamma (Ch. 20), all of which the pixels constrain and a spectrum does not. $\eqref{eq:thetaE-sv}$ is the back-of-the-envelope check every lensing paper runs before trusting an imaging fit — not a replacement for one.

Mass inside θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}}

Equation $\eqref{eq:alpha-kbar}$’s defining fact, κ‾(θE)=1\bar\kappa(\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) = 1, means the average surface density inside the Einstein radius is exactly Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} — regardless of whether the true profile is an SIS, an SIE, a cored halo, or anything else circularly averaged. So the enclosed mass follows from geometry alone:

M(<θE)=Σcr⋅πRE2,RE=DdθE, M(<\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) = \Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}\cdot\pi R_{\mathrm{E}}^2, \qquad R_{\mathrm{E}} = D_{\mathrm{d}}\,\theta_{\mathrm{E}},

implemented at site/guide_src/cosmo.py:66. This is the reason M(<θE)M(<\theta_{\mathrm{E}}), not the density slope, is what every lensing paper reports with confidence.

You already know this

M(<θE)M(<\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) is a checksum, not a fit. It depends only on the total enclosed inside a fixed boundary, never on how that total is arranged within it — the same way a histogram’s cumulative count up to a bin edge is fixed by the counts below it and is completely blind to which bin each of those counts landed in. γ\gamma is a claim about the shape inside that boundary; M(<θE)M(<\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) is a claim about the sum, and sums are far more robust to being wrong about the shape.

Ch. 15 already computed this for the Carousel cluster lens (Sheu et al. 2024): zl=0.49z_l=0.49, θE=13.03″\theta_{\mathrm{E}}=13.03'' with respect to zs=1.432z_s=1.432, giving Σcr=2.376×1015M⊙/Mpc2\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}} = 2.376\times10^{15}\ M_\odot/\mathrm{Mpc}^2 and M(<θE)=4.621×1013M⊙M(<\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) = 4.621\times10^{13}\ M_\odot . Sheu et al.’s own published fit reports 4.78×1013M⊙4.78\times10^{13}\ M_\odot (reproductions/sheu-2024b/README.md:24) — a ratio of 0.96670.9667 , 3.3%3.3\% low. That residual is not evidence against the identity; it is the price of the formula above assuming a circular aperture, while the real lens is an elliptical EPL with q=0.87q=0.87 and external shear γext=0.11\gamma_{\mathrm{ext}} = 0.11 (reproductions/sheu-2024b/README.md:20–22) — exactly what the repository’s own reproduction says drives the gap (reproductions/sheu-2024b/README.md:46). Feed the published best-fit parameters, ellipticity and all, into a real ray-traced lens model instead of the circular formula, and the same reproduction’s own deflection-based check of κ‾(θE)\bar\kappa(\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) — literally α(θE)/θE\alpha(\theta_{\mathrm{E}})/\theta_{\mathrm{E}}, the left-hand side of this chapter’s central identity, read off a fitted lenstronomy model’s own analytic EPL deflection rather than the closed-form SIS quadrature above — returns 1.0011.001 (reproductions/sheu-2024b/README.md:45; source at reproductions/sheu-2024b/04_setup_multiplane.py:132–134). Two independent numerical routes, a hand-rolled SIS quadrature and a fitted multi-galaxy lenstronomy model, land on the same identity to three significant figures.

Exercises

Exercise 19.1 — the identity holds for every γ\gamma, not just the SIS

The general EPL convergence (site/guide_src/lensing.py:81, circular case q=1q=1) is κ(θ)=3−γ2(θE/θ)γ−1\kappa(\theta) = \frac{3-\gamma}{2}\left(\theta_{\mathrm{E}}/\theta\right)^{\gamma-1}. Using $\eqref{eq:alpha-kbar}$, show that κ‾(θE)=1\bar\kappa(\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) = 1 for every value of γ<3\gamma < 3 — not just the isothermal γ=2\gamma=2 case worked out in the main text — and say in one sentence what this implies about how much information θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}} alone carries about γ\gamma.

Solution

κ‾(θ)=2θ2∫0θ3−γ2(θEt)γ−1tdt=(3−γ)θEγ−1θ2∫0θt2−γdt=(3−γ)θEγ−1θ2⋅θ3−γ3−γ=(θEθ)γ−1. \bar\kappa(\theta) = \frac{2}{\theta^2}\int_0^\theta \frac{3-\gamma}{2} \left(\frac{\theta_{\mathrm{E}}}{t}\right)^{\gamma-1} t\, dt = \frac{(3-\gamma)\,\theta_{\mathrm{E}}^{\gamma-1}}{\theta^2} \int_0^\theta t^{2-\gamma}\, dt = \frac{(3-\gamma)\,\theta_{\mathrm{E}}^{\gamma-1}}{\theta^2}\cdot \frac{\theta^{3-\gamma}}{3-\gamma} = \left(\frac{\theta_{\mathrm{E}}}{\theta}\right)^{\gamma-1}.

At θ=θE\theta = \theta_{\mathrm{E}} this is 1γ−1=11^{\gamma-1} = 1, independent of γ\gamma. (Setting γ=2\gamma=2 recovers κ‾(θ)=θE/θ\bar\kappa(\theta) = \theta_{\mathrm{E}}/\theta, exactly twice the SIS’s own κ(θ)=θE/(2θ)\kappa(\theta) = \theta_{\mathrm{E}}/(2\theta) from the main text — consistent with what the θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}}-from-σv\sigma_v derivation found directly.) Because every circular EPL, whatever its γ\gamma, satisfies κ‾(θE)=1\bar\kappa(\theta_{\mathrm{E}})=1 at its own θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}}, a measurement of θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}} alone carries essentially zero information about γ\gamma — the two are cleanly separated by construction. That separation is exactly why Ch. 20 onward needs the full image, not just the ring radius, to pin γ\gamma down.

Exercise 19.2 — rebuild θE=1.145″\theta_{\mathrm{E}} = 1.145'' by hand

Using only Ch. 15’s already-computed distances Dd(z=0.5)=1259.08D_{\mathrm{d}}(z=0.5)=1259.08 Mpc , Ds(z=2.0)=1726.62D_{\mathrm{s}}(z=2.0)=1726.62 Mpc , and Dds(0.5,2.0)=1097.08D_{\mathrm{ds}}(0.5,2.0)=1097.08 Mpc , plug σv=250\sigma_v=250 km/s into $\eqref{eq:thetaE-sv}$ and reproduce this chapter’s θE=1.145″\theta_{\mathrm{E}} = 1.145'' worked example without calling cosmo.py at all.

Solution

DdsDs=1097.081726.62≈0.6354,(σvc)2=(250299,792.458)2≈6.954×10−7. \frac{D_{\mathrm{ds}}}{D_{\mathrm{s}}} = \frac{1097.08}{1726.62} \approx 0.6354, \qquad \left(\frac{\sigma_v}{c}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{250}{299{,}792.458}\right)^2 \approx 6.954\times10^{-7}.

θE=4π×6.954×10−7×0.6354rad≈5.553×10−6rad. \theta_{\mathrm{E}} = 4\pi \times 6.954\times10^{-7} \times 0.6354\ \text{rad} \approx 5.553\times10^{-6}\ \text{rad}.

Multiply by 206,264.806206{,}264.806 arcsec/rad (Ch. 9) to get θE≈1.145″\theta_{\mathrm{E}} \approx 1.145'' , matching the worked example exactly — the whole formula, run by hand with a calculator, using nothing this chapter has not already derived.

Exercise 19.3 — the Einstein cross’s own redshifts

Repeat the Cikota calculation from the main text, but with the system’s own spectroscopic redshifts, zL1=0.636z_{\mathrm{L1}}=0.636, zs=2.597z_s=2.597 (reproductions/cikota-2023/papers/main.tex:166), instead of the illustrative pair used there. Run cosmo.theta_e_from_sigma_v(347.0, 0.636, 2.597) and compare the result to the repository’s own imaging fit of 2.103″2.103''. Then explain why it does not land exactly on 2.103″2.103'', given that 347347 km/s was itself obtained by inverting $\eqref{eq:thetaE-sv}$ at essentially this same geometry.

Solution 
import cosmo
cosmo.theta_e_from_sigma_v(347.0, 0.636, 2.597)   # roughly 2.12"

That lands far closer to the repository’s own 2.103″2.103'' imaging fit than the 2.233″2.233'' illustrative-pair result did — as it should, since this is now the right geometry. It is still not an exact match, because cosmo.py fixes cosmology at H0=70H_0=70, Ωm=0.3\Omega_m=0.3 throughout (site/guide_src/cosmo.py:29) — the convention the repository’s other cosmology-dependent reproductions share — while reproductions/cikota-2023 follows its own paper in adopting Planck18 (H0=67.4H_0=67.4, Ωm=0.315\Omega_m=0.315) for this specific conversion. Swap in H0=67.4H_0=67.4 and the small residual gap closes almost entirely. The lesson is not that $\eqref{eq:thetaE-sv}$ is imprecise; it is that which cosmology you plug in is itself an input worth tracking, the same point Ch. 14 makes about Ωm\Omega_m in general.

Exercise 19.4 — is the 3.3% mass gap a problem?

Ch. 15’s circular-aperture estimate, M(<θE)=4.621×1013M⊙M(<\theta_{\mathrm{E}}) = 4.621\times10^{13}\ M_\odot, sits 3.3%3.3\% below Sheu et al.’s published 4.78×1013M⊙4.78\times10^{13}\ M_\odot. Using this chapter’s mean-convergence identity, argue whether that gap should worry you about the identity itself, and what it would mean if the gap were instead 30%30\%.

Solution

The identity κ‾(θE)=1\bar\kappa(\theta_{\mathrm{E}})=1 was derived for a circularly symmetric lens; the real Carousel lens is an elliptical EPL (q=0.87q=0.87) plus external shear (γext=0.11\gamma_{\mathrm{ext}}=0.11), so πRE2\pi R_{\mathrm{E}}^2 is only an approximation to the true enclosed area, and a few percent of discrepancy is exactly what that approximation should cost — confirmed by the repository’s own independent deflection-based check landing at 1.0011.001 (reproductions/sheu-2024b/README.md:45), which uses the actual elliptical model rather than the circular formula and closes almost all of the gap. A 3.3%3.3\% mismatch is the ellipticity correction, not a crack in the identity. A 30%30\% mismatch would be a different matter — ellipticity this modest cannot move a profile-independent geometric quantity that far, so a gap that large would point at a wrong redshift, a wrong cosmology, or a real error in either θE\theta_{\mathrm{E}} or Σcr\Sigma_{\mathrm{cr}}, not at the assumption of circularity.

20. SIS, SIE, EPL: what γ\gamma actually means

Ch. 19 built the Einstein radius on top of one special mass profile — a circular, isothermal sphere — because that is the minimum object you need to make the definition concrete. This chapter takes the training wheels off, twice. First it lets the profile be elliptical instead of circular (SIS →\to SIE), because no real galaxy is circular on the sky. Then it lets the density slope itself vary instead of being fixed at “isothermal” (SIE →\to EPL), because that slope, called γ\gamma, is the single number this whole repository’s final report exists to pin down. By the end of this chapter you can write down exactly what the claim “γ=1.103\gamma = 1.103” asserts about a galaxy’s mass, derive the one formula that normalizes it, and — because this repo uses the letter γ\gamma for three unrelated things — you will know, in every later chapter, which one is meant. This chapter also opens the γ\gamma Ledger formally: every later chapter that touches the money number adds a row.

What you can skip

You already own power laws, 2×22\times2 linear maps, and Taylor expansion to second order (Ch. 2). If you are comfortable with a doubled-angle (spin-2) representation of orientation — the same idea as an unsigned gradient direction or a structure-tensor eigenvector in computer vision — skim Ellipticity for the repo-specific numbers only. If you already trust Ch. 5’s Jacobian decomposition A=(1−κ)I−ΓA = (1-\kappa)I - \Gamma, skim External shear for the same reason.

SIS to SIE

The singular isothermal sphere (SIS) from Ch. 10 has convergence κSIS(θ)=θE/(2θ)\kappa_{\mathrm{SIS}}(\theta) = \theta_{\mathrm{E}}/(2\theta) and — Ch. 6 hands you this fact without proving it — a deflection of constant modulus, 𝛂=θE𝛉̂\boldsymbol\alpha = \theta_{\mathrm{E}}\hat{\boldsymbol\theta} (site/guide_src/lensing.py:54). Here is the proof, and it is short because it reuses machinery you already have. For any circularly symmetric lens, Ch. 6’s ∇2ψ=2κ\nabla^2\psi=2\kappa, written out as the radial Laplacian of a function that depends only on θ\theta, together with α=dψ/dθ\alpha = d\psi/d\theta, is 1θddθ(θα(θ))=2κ(θ)\frac{1}{\theta}\frac{d}{d\theta}\!\big(\theta\,\alpha(\theta)\big) = 2\kappa(\theta). Integrate both sides from 00 to θ\theta:

θα(θ)=∫0θ2κ(t)tdt=θ2κ‾(θ)⇒α(θ)=θκ‾(θ), \theta\,\alpha(\theta) \;=\; \int_0^\theta 2\kappa(t)\,t\,dt \;=\; \theta^2\,\bar\kappa(\theta) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \alpha(\theta) \;=\; \theta\,\bar\kappa(\theta),

using Ch. 19’s own definition of κ‾\bar\kappa in the last step. This is a 2-D Newton’s shell theorem: the deflection at radius θ\theta depends only on the mean convergence enclosed, never on how that mass is arranged inside. For the SIS, κ‾SIS(θ)=θE/θ\bar\kappa_{\mathrm{SIS}}(\theta) = \theta_{\mathrm{E}}/\theta (the same power law as κ\kappa itself, one section below), so α(θ)=θ⋅(θE/θ)=θE\alpha(\theta) = \theta\cdot(\theta_{\mathrm{E}}/\theta) = \theta_{\mathrm{E}} — every θ\theta cancels, leaving a deflection that does not know how far out you are. That is a special, γ=2\gamma=2-specific coincidence, not a generic property of power-law lenses; the general case returns in the next section.

Real galaxies, including every lens this repository models, are not circular — light and mass both trace out ellipses on the sky. The natural next model keeps the isothermal (γ=2\gamma=2) density law but flattens its iso-density contours into ellipses of axis ratio qq: the singular isothermal ellipsoid (SIE). Its deflection has a standard closed form from the lensing literature, implemented at site/guide_src/lensing.py:65:

αx=θEq1−q2arctan⁡(1−q2xψ+s),αy=θEq1−q2artanh⁡(1−q2yψ+q2s), \alpha_x = \frac{\theta_{\mathrm E}\,q}{\sqrt{1-q^2}}\arctan\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{1-q^2}\,x}{\psi+s}\right), \qquad \alpha_y = \frac{\theta_{\mathrm E}\,q}{\sqrt{1-q^2}}\operatorname{artanh}\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{1-q^2}\,y}{\psi+q^2 s}\right),

with ψ=q2(x2+s2)+y2\psi = \sqrt{q^2(x^2+s^2)+y^2}, (x,y)(x,y) already rotated into the frame aligned with the ellipse’s own axes (lensing.py‘s _rotate handles turning the position angle ϕ\phi in and back out around this formula), and ss a small core radius that regularizes the point-mass singularity at the center. Gigalens’ own sie.py defines the identical constant, s_scale = 1e-4 (vendor/gigalens-sean/.../mass/sie.py:11) — but a same-named local variable shadows it to 00 one line into _param_conv (:16), so gigalens’ own SIE actually runs with zero core radius; only the unused class attribute matches lensing.py‘s choice, not gigalens’ executed behavior. Deriving that closed form is a genuine complex-analysis exercise (integrating an elliptical isothermal potential); this guide takes it as a fact and checks the one property that matters: at q→1q\to1, the SIE must reduce to the SIS. lensing.sie_deflection and lensing.sis_deflection, evaluated at the same point (θx,θy)=(0.6,0.8)″(\theta_x,\theta_y)=(0.6,0.8)'' (so r=θE=1″r=\theta_{\mathrm{E}}=1''), agree to within 0.057″0.057'' at q=0.9q=0.9 and to within 0.00064″0.00064'' at q=0.999q=0.999 — shrinking roughly in proportion to 1−q1-q, as the closed form’s own 1−q2\sqrt{1-q^2} factors predict. It does not shrink to machine zero, because sie_deflection clips qq at 0.999990.99999 internally and carries a nonzero core s=10−4s=10^{-4} by default (lensing.py:65,73) — a real numerical seam, not a bug: the exact q=1q=1 limit is a removable singularity in the formula, and the code sidesteps computing it by staying a hair away from it.

The EPL and gamma

The SIE fixed the density slope at γ=2\gamma=2. Ch. 10 already flagged that real ellipticals only cluster near isothermal, not sit exactly on it — so the campaign’s actual mass model promotes γ\gamma from a constant to a free parameter, giving the elliptical power law (EPL): the same isothermal ellipsoid, generalized to ρ(r)∼r−γ\rho(r)\sim r^{-\gamma} for any γ\gamma. Ch. 3 already derived the exponent this profile projects to: Σ(R)∼R1−γ\Sigma(R)\sim R^{1-\gamma}, hence κ(R)∼R1−γ\kappa(R)\sim R^{1-\gamma}, for any γ\gamma — that chapter also showed that the exponent’s own literal amplitude, 2AI(γ)2A\,I(\gamma) in Ch. 3, Eq. 3.1, blows up for an idealized, untruncated halo as γ→1+\gamma\to1^+ (the pp-test threshold on I(γ)I(\gamma)), and explicitly left this chapter the job of saying where the campaign’s actual prefactor, (3−γ)/2(3-\gamma)/2, comes from.

It comes from Ch. 19’s identity, not from that divergent integral. Posit κ(R)=A(γ)(θE/R)γ−1\kappa(R) = A(\gamma)\,(\theta_{\mathrm E}/R)^{\gamma-1} — the right exponent, an undetermined amplitude — and demand that κ‾(θE)=1\bar\kappa(\theta_{\mathrm E})=1, the defining property of the Einstein radius for any profile. Integrating exactly as in the SIS derivation above,

κ‾(θ)=2θ2∫0θAθEγ−1t1−γtdt=2A3−γ(θEθ)γ−1, \bar\kappa(\theta) = \frac{2}{\theta^2}\int_0^\theta A\,\theta_{\mathrm E}^{\gamma-1}t^{1-\gamma}\,t\,dt = \frac{2A}{3-\gamma}\left(\frac{\theta_{\mathrm E}}{\theta}\right)^{\gamma-1},

so κ‾(θE)=2A/(3−γ)\bar\kappa(\theta_{\mathrm E}) = 2A/(3-\gamma); setting this to 11 gives A=(3−γ)/2A = (3-\gamma)/2 — exactly the constant epl_kappa uses (site/guide_src/lensing.py:81):

κ(R)=3−γ2(θER)γ−1. \kappa(R) \;=\; \frac{3-\gamma}{2}\left(\frac{\theta_{\mathrm E}}{R}\right)^{\gamma-1}.

This normalization sidesteps Ch. 3’s divergence entirely: it is fixed by a convention (mean interior κ=1\kappa=1 at one radius), not by integrating an infinite halo, so it stays perfectly finite for every γ\gamma the prior allows — including exactly at γ=1\gamma=1. Gigalens’ own EPL implementation uses the identical exponent under the lenstronomy convention t=γ−1t=\gamma-1 (vendor/gigalens-sean/.../mass/epl.py:24); site/guide_src/lensing.py is deliberately not a wrapper around it, but the convergence law is the same law.

Two facts fall out of this derivation for free. First, setting R=θER=\theta_{\mathrm E} in the boxed formula gives the local convergence right at the Einstein ring: κ(θE)=(3−γ)/2\kappa(\theta_{\mathrm E}) = (3-\gamma)/2 — a different number from the mean interior convergence, which is exactly 11 for every γ\gamma by construction. At γ=2\gamma=2 (isothermal) these give 0.50.5 : the density right at an isothermal Einstein ring is exactly half the mean density inside it. Second, at γ=1\gamma=1 exactly, the exponent γ−1\gamma-1 vanishes and κ(R)=1\kappa(R) = 1 for every RR, not just at θE\theta_{\mathrm E} — a perfectly finite, spatially uniform sheet. That is the critical mass sheet: Ch. 21 shows a uniform κ=1\kappa=1 sheet is invisible to every imaging observable, the single most degenerate mass distribution in all of lensing. So γ=1\gamma=1 is a wall in two related but distinct senses — Ch. 3’s sense (an idealized untruncated halo’s total surface density literally diverges there) and this chapter’s sense (even the finite, correctly normalized model becomes totally unidentifiable there) — and the campaign’s own prior, gamma=tfd.TruncatedNormal(2.0, 0.25, 1.0, 2.7) (reproductions/claude-giga-lens/cgl/e2.py:110), places its hard floor at exactly that boundary.

Hold that against the money number. γbinned(corr,low)=1.103\gamma_{\mathrm{binned}}(\mathrm{corr,low})=1.103 gives κ(θE)=0.9485\kappa(\theta_{\mathrm E}) = 0.9485 — only 0.05150.0515 short of the fully degenerate sheet’s κ(θE)=1\kappa(\theta_{\mathrm E})=1 , and well past isothermal’s own 0.50.5 on the way there. Ch. 10 already flagged this value as 3.5883.588 prior-sigma from isothermal ; this is a sharper, structural way to be worried about the same number, because it says something about identifiability, not just prior surprise. The anchor, γ=1.433\gamma=1.433 , sits at κ(θE)=0.7835\kappa(\theta_{\mathrm E})=0.7835 — a real departure from isothermal, but nowhere near the degenerate wall. The fine-product artifact, γ=2.585\gamma=2.585 , sits at 0.20750.2075 , on the opposite, steep side. All four values share the same mean interior convergence, exactly 11 at θE\theta_{\mathrm E} — that identity, checked here for the money slope by direct quadrature, does not care what γ\gamma is; only the local number does.

The gamma overload, paid in full

This repository uses the single glyph γ\gamma for three unrelated objects, and the report’s own authors clearly knew it: reproductions/claude-giga-lens/papers/main.tex defines separate macros for each (lines 24–27: \gammaEPL, \gext, \gextone, \gexttwo). This guide mirrors that discipline exactly:

  1. Bare γ\gamma — the EPL’s 3-D density slope, ρ∼r−γ\rho\sim r^{-\gamma}, this section’s subject and the campaign’s money parameter. This is the only meaning bare γ\gamma ever carries in this guide.
  2. γext\gamma_{\mathrm{ext}} — the external shear’s magnitude, the next section’s subject. Never bare γ\gamma, never γsh\gamma_{sh}.
  3. γ1,γ2\gamma_1,\gamma_2 — shear components. These name two different but related quantities depending on context: Ch. 5’s traceless part of a Jacobian (A=(1−κ)I−ΓA=(1-\kappa)I-\Gamma, computed from whatever deflection field you differentiate), or the external-shear model’s own two parameters (next section). The next section shows these literally coincide when the external field is isolated — but not in general, since a full EPL+shear Jacobian sums a spatially varying piece (from the EPL) and a constant piece (from the shear). Wherever both could appear in the same breath, this guide subscripts the external one: γext,1,γext,2\gamma_{\mathrm{ext},1},\gamma_{\mathrm{ext},2}.

Ellipticity

Every ellipse in this repository’s model — the EPL mass, the SIE, and every one of the four lens-light Sersic components plus the source — is parameterized the same way: not by (q,ϕ)(q,\phi) directly, but by a pair (e1,e2)(e_1,e_2) that gigalens’ epl.py and sie.py both convert identically, implemented once at site/guide_src/lensing.py:32:

ϕ=12atan2⁡(e2,e1),c=|e|=e12+e22,q=1−c1+c. \phi = \tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{atan2}(e_2,e_1), \qquad c = |e| = \sqrt{e_1^2+e_2^2}, \qquad q = \frac{1-c}{1+c}.

The half-angle is not a stylistic choice. Write the complex ellipticity ϵ=e1+ie2\epsilon = e_1+ie_2. If c=|ϵ|c=|\epsilon| is fixed, the map ϕ↦ϵ=ce2iϕ\phi\mapsto\epsilon=c\,e^{2i\phi} sends a full 180∘180^\circ rotation of the position angle, ϕ→ϕ+π\phi\to\phi+\pi, to ϵe2πi=ϵ\epsilon\,e^{2\pi i}=\epsilon — the identical complex number. That has to be true: an ellipse has no arrowhead, so rotating it by 180∘180^\circ produces the same ellipse, and the parameterization had better not invent a difference where there is none. A quarter turn, ϕ→ϕ+π/2\phi\to\phi+\pi/2, is a different story — it swaps which axis is which, and ϵ\epsilon must change: ϵeiπ=−ϵ\epsilon\,e^{i\pi}=-\epsilon.

Take (e1,e2)=(0.3,0.4)(e_1,e_2)=(0.3,0.4) — a 3-4-5 triangle, chosen for clean numbers, not a typical draw from the mass ellipticity’s own prior (e1,e2 ~ Normal(0, 0.1), cgl/e2.py:111, a few times smaller). ellip_to_q_phi gives q=1/3q = 1/3 and ϕ=26.565∘\phi = 26.565^\circ . Reconstructing ϵ\epsilon at ϕ+π\phi+\pi with the same c=(1−q)/(1+q)=0.5c=(1-q)/(1+q)=0.5 reproduces e1=0.3e_1=0.3 exactly — the invariance holds to floating-point precision, as the algebra above promised — while reconstructing at ϕ+π/2\phi+\pi/2 flips the sign, e1=−0.3e_1=-0.3 .

You already know this

This is exactly the doubled-angle trick used everywhere an “orientation” has no arrowhead — a line, an edge, a nematic director. A structure tensor’s dominant eigenvector in image processing is conventionally reported mod π\pi, not mod 2π2\pi, for the identical reason: an unsigned gradient direction and its 180∘180^\circ-rotated twin describe the same edge. Spin-2 is the physics name for a doubled-angle representation you have almost certainly already coded.

External shear

Mass sitting outside the modeled lens galaxy — a companion, the group or cluster environment, structure along the line of sight — still bends light, but its potential ψext(x,y)\psi_{\mathrm{ext}}(x,y) near the lens center is smooth and slowly varying compared to the galaxy’s own steep potential. Taylor-expand it to second order (Ch. 2): the constant term is an unobservable overall phase, the linear term is a uniform image shift indistinguishable from moving the source (an unobservable degeneracy), so the first term with any observable content is the quadratic one — a constant Hessian. If none of that external mass is itself sitting at the lens plane within the modeled region, Ch. 6’s ∇2ψ=2κ\nabla^2\psi=2\kappa forces the trace of that constant Hessian to vanish locally, leaving only its traceless part: a spatially uniform shear, (γext,1,γext,2)(\gamma_{\mathrm{ext},1},\gamma_{\mathrm{ext},2}), and nothing else. That is the external-shear model, shear_deflection (site/guide_src/lensing.py:93):

αx=γext,1x+γext,2y,αy=γext,2x−γext,1y. \alpha_x = \gamma_{\mathrm{ext},1}\,x+\gamma_{\mathrm{ext},2}\,y, \qquad \alpha_y = \gamma_{\mathrm{ext},2}\,x-\gamma_{\mathrm{ext},1}\,y.

The campaign’s own prior draws each component independently, γ1,γ2∼Normal(0,0.05)\gamma_1,\gamma_2\sim\mathrm{Normal}(0,0.05) (reproductions/claude-giga-lens/cgl/e2.py:113–114) — note the code’s bare parameter names, exactly the collision this chapter’s ledger warned about; in this guide’s notation those are γext,1,γext,2\gamma_{\mathrm{ext},1},\gamma_{\mathrm{ext},2}. If you want the shear quoted as a single magnitude-and-angle pair the way γext\gamma_{\mathrm{ext}} is defined in the notation contract, it is γext=γext,12+γext,22\gamma_{\mathrm{ext}}=\sqrt{\gamma_{\mathrm{ext},1}^2+\gamma_{\mathrm{ext},2}^2} — the shear’s own analogue of ellipticity’s c=|e|c=|e| above.

Differentiate shear_deflection alone with lens_jacobian (Ch. 5’s numerical Jacobian, applied here to a deflection field that has nothing else in it) at one plausible draw, γext,1=0.03,γext,2=−0.02\gamma_{\mathrm{ext},1}=0.03,\ \gamma_{\mathrm{ext},2}=-0.02 (so γext=0.036056\gamma_{\mathrm{ext}}=0.036056 ), evaluated at an arbitrary point (0.4,0.7)″(0.4,0.7)'': kappa_gamma_from_jacobian recovers κ=0\kappa=0 , γ1=0.03\gamma_1=0.03 , and γ2=−0.02\gamma_2=-0.02 — exactly the input, to machine precision, at every point you would care to check, because αx,αy\alpha_x,\alpha_y are linear in (x,y)(x,y) and a linear map’s own derivative has no remainder to miss (Ch. 2’s point about Taylor expansion, cashed out as a finite-difference check with zero truncation error). This is the resolution the overload warning promised: external shear is not a new kind of object, it is Ch. 5’s (γ1,γ2)(\gamma_1,\gamma_2) decomposition of the total Jacobian, restricted to just the one additive, spatially constant term that an external tidal field contributes. In a full EPL+shear fit, the total Jacobian sums this constant piece with the EPL’s own spatially varying convergence and shear — the two notions of γ1,γ2\gamma_1,\gamma_2 genuinely coincide only when you isolate the external term this way, which is exactly why the notation contract insists on the subscript everywhere else. One further honest note: an external shear’s stretch and the lens’s own ellipticity both distort images in visually similar ways, and disentangling the two from imaging data alone is a real, separate degeneracy — Ch. 21 is where degeneracies of this kind get a full treatment; this chapter only flags it.

Source models

Everything so far describes the lens: the foreground galaxy’s mass (EPL + shear) and light (four Sersic components, Ch. 10). The source — the background galaxy actually being lensed, whose light, run through the lens equation, produces the arcs and rings Ch. 22 fits pixel by pixel — needs its own light model, and a single Sersic profile is not flexible enough: real source galaxies have clumps, spiral structure, and asymmetries no smooth elliptical profile captures. The campaign’s source model is a Sersic component (its own independent e1,e2∼TruncatedNormal(0,0.15,−0.5,0.5)e_1,e_2\sim\mathrm{TruncatedNormal}(0,0.15,-0.5,0.5), a third distinct ellipticity prior alongside the mass’s Normal(0,0.1)\mathrm{Normal}(0,0.1) and the lens light’s TruncatedNormal(0,0.15,−0.4,0.4)\mathrm{TruncatedNormal}(0,0.15,-0.4,0.4); cgl/e2.py:120–125) plus a shapelet expansion layered on top.

Shapelets are 2-D Gauss–Hermite basis functions — a Gaussian envelope times a Hermite polynomial in xx and yy, truncated at total polynomial order nmaxn_{\max} (vendor/gigalens-sean/.../light/shapelets.py:19). At nmax=6n_{\max}=6 — the campaign’s choice — the count of independent modes is the triangular number (nmax+1)(nmax+2)/2=28(n_{\max}+1)(n_{\max}+2)/2 = 28 , matching the model’s own docstring, “Sersic + Shapelets(nmax=6n_{\max}=6) source with 28 EXPLICIT amps” (reproductions/claude-giga-lens/cgl/e2.py:13), each with an independent amplitude parameter and its own Gaussian prior (cgl/e2.py:126–131).

You already know this

A truncated orthogonal basis layered on top of a smooth parametric fit to catch residual structure is a move you have made before, whatever you called it — a low-order DCT or wavelet expansion of a residual image, a handful of extra principal components kept after the dominant ones. The physics content here is only which basis (2-D Hermite functions under a Gaussian weight, not sines or wavelets) and how many terms.

Because each shapelet amplitude multiplies a fixed rendered image and the 28 contributions simply sum, these amplitudes enter the forward model linearly — unlike γ\gamma, qq, ϕ\phi, or any of the profile shape parameters above, all of which enter nonlinearly. That linearity is exactly what Ch. 22 exploits: the 28 amplitudes get integrated out analytically (a ridge-regularized normal equation, reproductions/claude-giga-lens/cgl/marg.py) rather than sampled, which is why the campaign’s sampled parameter count drops from 74 dimensions to 46 (cgl/e2.py:13). This chapter only names the 28 parameters being marginalized; deriving the marginalization itself is Ch. 22’s job.

γ Ledger

What this chapter rules in or out about γ=1.103\gamma = 1.103: nothing empirically — no data enters this chapter, only definitions. What it does establish is the structural stakes. γ=1\gamma=1 is not an arbitrary round number for the prior’s hard wall: it is exactly where the EPL’s local convergence at θE\theta_{\mathrm E} becomes a spatially uniform sheet, the most degenerate mass distribution lensing can produce (Ch. 21). The money number’s own κ(θE)=0.9485\kappa(\theta_{\mathrm E})=0.9485 sits only 0.05150.0515 short of it — a sharper, more structural way to read its closeness to the wall than Ch. 10’s 3.5883.588-prior-sigma framing , though both point at the same number. Whether the data genuinely demand a profile sitting that close to degenerate, or whether some part of the pipeline pushed it there artificially, is not this chapter’s question — it belongs to Ch. 21, Ch. 25, and Ch. 26.
